questions.title: Writing a Revenue Measure That Plain SUM Can't Express
questions.prompt: Sales[Quantity] and Sales[UnitPrice] exist as separate columns, but there's no stored Revenue column. Write a measure that totals revenue, filtered to only rows where the related SalesTerritory[Country] isn't the United States, and explain why SUM alone cannot do this.
questions.modelAnswer: Plain SUM only aggregates a single existing column directly - it has nothing to point at here, because revenue is a per-row computation (Quantity times UnitPrice), not a stored value. SUMX is an iterator: it walks the table row by row, evaluates an expression using that row's own values, then adds up the results - exactly what's needed to compute Quantity times UnitPrice fresh for each row before summing. Combining SUMX with FILTER handles the country condition: FILTER returns the subset of Sales rows where the related country isn't 'United States,' reached via RELATED since Country lives on the territory table, and SUMX then iterates only that filtered subset rather than the whole table. SUM alone can express neither the per-row multiplication nor the conditional subset - both require row-by-row evaluation, which is the entire reason the X-suffixed iterator functions exist.
questions.professionalAnswer: SUM can only point at a single column that already exists, and revenue here doesn't exist as a column - it only exists as Quantity times UnitPrice computed per row. That's exactly what SUMX is for: it goes row by row, computes that multiplication fresh each time, and adds the results together. To handle the country exclusion, I'd wrap the table argument in a FILTER that uses RELATED to reach the territory table's Country column from each Sales row, and SUMX then only iterates over the rows that pass. There's really no way to get SUM to do either of those two things - the per-row math or the conditional subset - because SUM was never built to evaluate an expression, only to add up a column that's already there.
questions.code:
Non-USA Revenue =
SUMX(
    FILTER(
        Sales,
        RELATED(SalesTerritory[Country]) <> "United States"
    ),
    Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]
)
questions.example: Contrast: Total Revenue = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]) with no FILTER would total revenue across every country; adding the FILTER narrows the exact rows SUMX iterates.
commonMistakes: Trying to write SUM(Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice]) directly - SUM doesn't accept an expression, only a single column
Forgetting RELATED is needed to reach the country column on a different table from inside the row-by-row FILTER condition
Not realizing FILTER's second argument is itself evaluated in row context per row of Sales
Using a calculated column instead of a measure, pre-computing per-row revenue and losing the ability to recompute dynamically under different filter contexts
keyPoints: SUMX evaluates an expression row by row, then sums the results
Use SUMX whenever the needed value isn't a single stored column
FILTER inside SUMX's table argument narrows which rows get iterated
RELATED reaches a related table's column from inside row context

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct SUMX + FILTER + RELATED expression
Explains why SUM alone cannot express this
Explains the role of FILTER narrowing the iterated rows
Explains RELATED's role in reaching the related table

questions.title: Rewriting a YoY Growth Measure With Variables
questions.prompt: Rewrite this measure to follow DAX best practices, and explain each change: Sales YoY Growth % = ([Sales] - CALCULATE([Sales], PARALLELPERIOD('Date'[Date], -12, MONTH))) / CALCULATE([Sales], PARALLELPERIOD('Date'[Date], -12, MONTH))
questions.code:
Sales YoY Growth %% =
VAR SalesPriorYear =
    CALCULATE ( [Sales], PARALLELPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], -12, MONTH ) )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( [Sales] - SalesPriorYear, SalesPriorYear )
questions.modelAnswer: Two problems, two fixes. First, CALCULATE([Sales], PARALLELPERIOD(...)) is written twice and evaluated twice - identical work done over again for no reason, which costs real query time on a large model. A VAR computes it once, names it, and both places that need it reference the stored result instead of recomputing it, roughly halving the work for this formula. Second, the plain '/' operator throws an error the instant the denominator is zero or blank, which happens for any period with no prior-year data - a new product line, a new store, the first year of history - and that error surfaces to end users as a broken visual instead of a clean blank. DIVIDE handles a zero/blank denominator gracefully, returning blank by default, or a value you specify, instead of erroring. Naming the variable SalesPriorYear also makes the RETURN line read as plain English instead of a repeated formula, which matters when someone else, or you in six months, has to maintain this.
questions.professionalAnswer: Two things jump out. The same CALCULATE/PARALLELPERIOD expression is written twice, which means the engine computes 'sales a year ago' twice for no reason - I'd pull that into a VAR, compute it once, and reference it in both places it's needed, which is real query-time savings, not just tidiness. The other issue is the plain division - the moment there's no prior-year data at all, which happens for anything new, that divide-by-zero throws an error straight into the visual instead of quietly returning blank. I'd swap it for DIVIDE, which handles that gracefully. On top of the performance and correctness fixes, naming the variable SalesPriorYear also just makes the RETURN line readable as a sentence instead of a repeated formula, which matters for anyone maintaining this later, including me.
questions.example: Debugging tip from the same pattern: temporarily change RETURN to just SalesPriorYear to inspect what the variable actually holds for a given filter context, before reinstating the real DIVIDE expression.
commonMistakes: Leaving the repeated CALCULATE/PARALLELPERIOD expression evaluated twice instead of once via a variable
Using plain division and letting the report error out on periods with no prior-year data
Naming variables generically (Var1, Result) instead of something that documents what the value represents
Not knowing the VAR-swap-to-RETURN trick for isolating which part of a formula produces an unexpected value
keyPoints: VAR/RETURN computes a repeated subexpression once instead of multiple times
DIVIDE avoids division-by-zero/blank errors that plain / throws
Named variables double as self-documentation
Temporarily returning a variable directly is a fast debugging technique

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct VAR/RETURN rewrite eliminating the duplicated CALCULATE call
Correct use of DIVIDE in place of /
Explains the performance benefit of computing once vs twice
Explains the zero/blank-denominator failure mode DIVIDE avoids

questions.title: Fix the Non-SARGable Order Lookup
questions.prompt: The query below is used in a nightly dashboard refresh and is now the slowest query in the job, taking almost 4 minutes against the Orders table (60M rows, nonclustered index on OrderDate). Rewrite it so it can use an index seek instead of a scan, without changing what it returns.
questions.code:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount
FROM Orders
WHERE CONVERT(varchar(10), OrderDate, 120) = '2026-03-15'
   OR DATEADD(day, 1, OrderDate) = '2026-03-16';
questions.modelAnswer: This query has two separate non-SARGable predicates combined with OR, each of which independently forces a full scan: CONVERT(varchar(10), OrderDate, 120) wraps the column in a string conversion before comparing it, and DATEADD(day, 1, OrderDate) performs arithmetic on the column before comparing it — both require per-row evaluation across all 60 million rows, and the OR compounds the cost further because the optimizer can't cleanly combine two non-seekable branches into a single seek plan. Both predicates are actually expressing the exact same intent (rows where OrderDate falls on March 15, 2026), so the correct fix is to collapse them into a single SARGable range predicate that leaves OrderDate bare on one side of the comparison, using a half-open interval to correctly capture the entire day regardless of time-of-day values stored in the column.
questions.professionalAnswer: Looking at this, both of these predicates are just two different, overcomplicated ways of saying 'OrderDate is March 15th, 2026' — one converts the column to a string and compares it to a string literal, the other adds a day and compares to the 16th, and both of those operations have to run against the column before SQL Server can even check the condition, which means it can't seek, it has to scan every row and compute the expression first. I'd collapse this down to a plain date range using the raw column, written as a half-open interval so it still works correctly even if OrderDate has a time component — that keeps the column bare on the left side of the comparison so the optimizer can seek straight into the nonclustered index on OrderDate instead of touching all 60 million rows.
questions.example:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount
FROM Orders
WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-03-15'
  AND OrderDate < '2026-03-16';
commonMistakes: Only fixing one of the two predicates and leaving the other non-SARGable branch in the OR
Using OrderDate = '2026-03-15' directly, which silently misses rows with a non-midnight time component
Not recognizing that both predicates express the same logical condition and can be merged into one range
Adding an index hint instead of fixing the predicate, which doesn't solve the underlying non-SARGable issue
Forgetting the half-open interval pattern and using BETWEEN with an inclusive end date/time that can miss late-day rows
keyPoints: Both original predicates wrap the column in a function/arithmetic, forcing per-row evaluation and a scan
Recognize that both branches express the same underlying date condition
Rewrite as a single SARGable half-open range on the bare column
Half-open range correctly handles any time-of-day component on OrderDate
Resulting plan should allow an index seek on the nonclustered OrderDate index

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies both predicates as non-SARGable and explains why
Produces a correct, equivalent SARGable rewrite
Uses a half-open interval that correctly handles time components
Explains expected improvement (seek vs scan)
Clean, correct SQL syntax

questions.title: Fix the Broken YTD Measure
questions.prompt: A YTD Sales measure is returning the same value for every month in a line chart instead of accumulating within each year. The model has a proper marked date table (Dates[Date]) related to Sales[OrderDate]. Diagnose and fix the DAX below.
questions.modelAnswer: The bug is that DATESYTD is being pointed at Sales[OrderDate] instead of the marked date table's date column, Dates[Date]. DATESYTD requires a contiguous, single-column date reference from a properly marked date table in order to correctly generate the set of dates from the start of the year up through the latest date in the current filter context — when you give it a column from a fact table like Sales[OrderDate], the function either errors in stricter scenarios or, if it technically runs, fails to produce the correct year-to-date date range because it isn't operating against the marked date dimension that the model's time intelligence relies on, which is why the result ends up static/incorrect across the visual rather than accumulating per period. The fix is to reference Dates[Date] (the date table's column) inside DATESYTD, relying on the active relationship between Dates[Date] and Sales[OrderDate] to propagate the resulting date filter onto the Sales table through normal filter propagation, exactly the way all of Power BI's built-in time intelligence functions expect to be used.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I see DATESYTD referencing a column straight off the fact table rather than the date table, that's the bug. Time intelligence functions like DATESYTD are built to work against a proper, contiguous date dimension — they need to generate the full date range from January 1st up to the current context's latest date, and they do that correctly only when pointed at the marked date table's date column. Pointing it at Sales[OrderDate] instead means it's not working with the dimension the model's time intelligence is built around, so instead of correctly expanding to 'every day from the start of this year through now,' it's not producing the right filtered date set at all, which is exactly why you're seeing the same number repeat across every month instead of accumulating. The fix is just to swap the reference to Dates[Date], and let the existing relationship between Dates[Date] and Sales[OrderDate] do its job of pushing that date filter down onto the Sales table like it would for any other filter.
questions.example:
YTD Sales =
CALCULATE(
    SUM(Sales[Amount]),
    DATESYTD(Dates[Date])
)
-- Dates[Date] must come from a table marked as the Date Table
-- in Power BI, with an active relationship to Sales[OrderDate].
commonMistakes: Referencing the fact table's date column instead of the marked date table's column inside time intelligence functions
Forgetting to actually mark the Dates table as a 'Date Table' in Model view, even if the column reference is fixed
Assuming a relationship alone (without 'Mark as Date Table') is sufficient for DATESYTD to work correctly
Not checking that the date table is contiguous (no missing calendar days) which DATESYTD also requires
Confusing DATESYTD's date range output with a value, forgetting it must be wrapped in CALCULATE with an aggregate
keyPoints: DATESYTD must reference the marked date table's column, not a fact table date column
The date table must be marked as a Date Table and be contiguous for correct results
Filter propagation from Dates[Date] to Sales[OrderDate] relies on the active relationship
CALCULATE wraps the aggregate while DATESYTD supplies the filtered date range
Symptom (flat/repeated values) is a strong signal of a broken time-intelligence date reference

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the root cause (wrong column reference)
Provides the correct fixed DAX
Explains the requirement for a marked, contiguous date table
Explains filter propagation via the relationship
Clarity

questions.title: Write an LOD Expression for First Purchase Date
questions.prompt: Using a Sales data source with Customer ID, Order Date, and Sales Amount, write a FIXED LOD calculated field that returns each customer's first purchase date, and then a second calculated field that flags whether a given order row IS that customer's first order. Explain how you'd use the flag to compute new-customer revenue versus repeat-customer revenue in a view broken down by Region, even when the view is filtered.
questions.modelAnswer: The first calculated field needs a FIXED LOD that computes the minimum Order Date per Customer ID, fixed at the customer grain regardless of whatever dimensions (like Region) happen to be on the view's shelves: FIXED [Customer ID]: MIN([Order Date]). The second field compares each row's own Order Date to that fixed first-purchase date and returns a boolean: [Order Date] = [First Purchase Date]. Because the FIXED calculation is computed at the data-source query level at the Customer ID grain, it is unaffected by whatever Region breakdown the view applies on top of it, which is exactly why this pattern correctly identifies the single first order per customer even inside a Region-sliced view — the LOD doesn't shrink to 'first order within this region,' it correctly reflects 'first order across all of that customer's history,' which is normally the intended business definition of a new customer. To split revenue by new vs. repeat, you'd use the Is First Order boolean as a dimension (or inside a CASE/IF) to bucket Sales Amount into two measures — SUM(IF [Is First Order] THEN [Sales Amount] END) for new-customer revenue and the ELSE branch for repeat revenue — and because the underlying FIXED LOD was computed before most ordinary filters apply (unless those filters are promoted to Context or specifically included in the LOD's dimension list), you need to be careful: if the view is filtered to a specific date range using an ordinary filter, the 'first purchase' definition may still reflect the customer's true first order even outside the filtered window, which is usually correct behavior for a new/repeat split, but should be explicitly validated against the specific business question being asked.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the first-purchase field, I'd write a FIXED LOD at the Customer ID grain — FIXED Customer ID, MIN of Order Date — which locks that calculation to 'this customer's earliest order ever,' completely independent of whatever's on the view. Then the 'is this their first order' flag is just a comparison — does this row's Order Date equal that fixed first-purchase date. The reason FIXED is the right tool here rather than a table calc is that I want this answer to stay stable no matter how someone slices the view by Region or Product or anything else — a table calc would recompute relative to whatever's visible, but I specifically want 'first order' to mean first order across their entire history, not first order within whatever's currently filtered. Once I've got that boolean flag, splitting revenue into new versus repeat is just a conditional aggregation — sum Sales Amount where the flag is true for new-customer revenue, sum it where false for repeat revenue, and I can break that down by Region on the same view. The one thing I'd flag to a stakeholder is the filter interaction — ordinary filters on the view generally run after this FIXED LOD is computed, so even if someone filters the view down to just this year, the 'first order' flag still reflects their true all-time first order, which is almost always what you want for a new-vs-repeat split, but it's worth being explicit about that so nobody's surprised when a 'new' customer in this year's filtered view turns out to have ordered years before and the flag still says 'not first order.'
commonMistakes: Using a table calculation instead of FIXED, causing the 'first order' definition to change depending on what's filtered/visible
Forgetting FIXED LOD evaluates before most ordinary filters, which can surprise stakeholders who expect it to shrink with the view's filters
Comparing dates with floating point/time precision issues instead of exact date matches
Not validating the new-vs-repeat split against a manually checked customer to confirm the flag behaves as expected
Using INCLUDE instead of FIXED, which would make the result sensitive to other dimensions on the view
keyPoints: FIXED LOD at Customer ID grain computes a stable, view-independent first purchase date
A boolean flag compares each row's Order Date to the FIXED first purchase date
FIXED LOD generally evaluates before ordinary (non-context) filters, which matters for the business definition
New/repeat revenue split uses conditional aggregation on the flag, can be broken down by any other dimension like Region
Business intent (true first-ever order vs. first-order-within-filtered-window) should be explicitly confirmed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct FIXED LOD syntax for first purchase date
Correct boolean flag comparing order date to first purchase date
Correct conditional aggregation for new vs repeat revenue by Region
Explains FIXED LOD's filter-order independence and why it matters here
Clear, valid Tableau calculation syntax

questions.title: Design a Tumbling Window Pipeline With Retry and Alerting
questions.prompt: You need an Azure Data Factory pipeline that ingests hourly batch files from a partner into Azure Data Lake, processes each hour's file exactly once even if the pipeline is paused and resumed, and alerts the team on repeated failure without manual babysitting. Describe the trigger type, retry configuration, and failure-handling pattern you'd configure, and explain why a tumbling window trigger is the right choice over a simple schedule trigger here.
questions.modelAnswer: A tumbling window trigger is the correct choice because it is explicitly designed around fixed, non-overlapping time windows that each get their own tracked execution state and window start/end time (@trigger().outputs.windowStartTime / windowEndTime), which lets the pipeline know precisely which hour's file it should be processing for that run, and critically, it supports dependency and retry semantics plus automatic backfill: if the pipeline is paused for several hours and then resumed, the tumbling window trigger will automatically queue and execute the missed windows in order, each exactly once, rather than simply skipping ahead to 'now' the way a plain schedule trigger would. A schedule trigger fires at wall-clock times with no concept of windows or backfill — if it's paused, those fire times are simply lost, and there's no built-in mechanism tying a given run to 'which hour's file' beyond what you manually derive from the trigger time, making exactly-once-per-hour semantics much harder to guarantee. For retry, I'd configure the trigger's own retryPolicy (count and interval) for transient failures at the trigger level, and additionally configure the Copy Activity's own retry count/interval for transient source/sink connectivity issues, since activity-level retries handle smaller transient hiccups without re-running the entire pipeline. For failure handling and alerting, I'd attach a failure-path activity (via the 'on failure' dependency condition in the pipeline canvas) that runs after the main activities only if they fail, which calls a Logic App or Azure Function to post to Teams/email, or more directly, configure an Azure Monitor alert rule on the Data Factory's own PipelineFailedRuns metric so the team gets paged without needing custom alerting logic embedded in every pipeline.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for a tumbling window trigger here specifically because of the backfill and exactly-once guarantees it gives you, which a plain schedule trigger just doesn't have. A schedule trigger is basically a clock — it fires at set wall-clock times, and if the pipeline's paused when a fire time comes around, that execution is just gone, there's no catch-up. A tumbling window trigger instead tracks discrete time windows, each with its own state, so if I pause it for six hours and then resume, it knows exactly which windows it missed and it'll queue them up and run them in order, each one exactly once — which is exactly the 'process each hour's file exactly once even after a pause' requirement here. Inside the pipeline, I'd use the trigger's own windowStartTime and windowEndTime parameters to construct the exact filename or path for that hour's partner file, so there's no ambiguity about which window a given run corresponds to. For retries, I'd set them at two levels — a retry policy on the trigger itself for the pipeline as a whole, and separately a retry count on the Copy Activity itself, since a lot of these partner-file failures are transient network blips that resolve themselves on a quick retry without needing to escalate. And for the 'alert without babysitting' part, I wouldn't build custom alerting logic inside the pipeline — I'd set an Azure Monitor alert rule directly against Data Factory's pipeline failure metrics, so once retries are exhausted and a run is truly failed, it pages the team through whatever channel they already use, rather than relying on someone checking the monitoring tab.
commonMistakes: Choosing a schedule trigger and manually trying to reconstruct 'which hour' logic from current wall-clock time
Assuming a paused schedule trigger will automatically backfill missed runs the way a tumbling window trigger does
Only configuring retries at the activity level and ignoring trigger-level retry policy, or vice versa
Building custom email/Teams alerting inside every pipeline instead of using Azure Monitor alert rules on Data Factory metrics
Not using windowStartTime/windowEndTime to deterministically identify which file/partition a given run should process
keyPoints: Tumbling window trigger tracks discrete, stateful time windows with automatic backfill on resume
windowStartTime/windowEndTime deterministically identify which hour's data a run should process
Retry should be configured at both the trigger level and the activity level for different failure classes
Azure Monitor alert rules on Data Factory metrics provide alerting without custom in-pipeline logic
Schedule triggers lack windowing/backfill semantics, making exactly-once-per-period harder to guarantee

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly justifies tumbling window trigger over schedule trigger with backfill/windowing reasoning
Correctly describes retry configuration at trigger and activity levels
Correctly describes a sound failure-alerting pattern
Uses windowStartTime/windowEndTime correctly to identify the processing window
Clarity and completeness

questions.title: Write a GitHub Actions Workflow to Run dbt Tests in CI
questions.prompt: Your team wants pull requests against the dbt project to automatically run `dbt build` and `dbt test` against a CI target before they can be merged, with the Snowflake credentials never appearing in plaintext anywhere in the repo. Write the GitHub Actions workflow YAML that achieves this, and explain how the credentials are kept secure.
questions.modelAnswer: The workflow needs to trigger on pull_request events targeting the relevant branch, check out the repository, set up Python, install dbt and its Snowflake adapter, and then run dbt build/dbt test against a CI-specific target — with every credential (account, user, password or key, warehouse, database) injected as environment variables sourced from GitHub Actions Secrets rather than written into dbt's profiles.yml or any committed file. GitHub Secrets are encrypted at rest, only decrypted into the runner's environment at execution time, masked in any log output automatically if they appear verbatim, and are scoped to the repository (or organization) so they're never visible in the workflow file itself or in pull request diffs — the workflow only references them by name (e.g., ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD }}), so even someone with read access to the YAML never sees the actual value. The profiles.yml used in CI should reference environment variables (via env_var() in dbt's Jinja) rather than literal credentials, which keeps the same profiles.yml file safe to commit to the repo. Branch protection rules should additionally require this workflow to pass as a required status check before merging, which is what actually enforces 'tests must pass before merge' rather than merely running the tests informationally.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set this up to trigger on pull_request, so it runs automatically whenever someone opens or updates a PR against the branch we care about. The workflow checks out the code, sets up Python, installs dbt-snowflake, and then runs dbt build followed by dbt test against a CI target defined in profiles.yml. The key thing for the credentials requirement is that nothing sensitive ever touches the repo in plaintext — I'd store the Snowflake account, user, password, warehouse, and database as encrypted Secrets in the GitHub repository settings, and reference them in the workflow only as ${{ secrets.SOMETHING }}. GitHub handles the encryption at rest, only injects the decrypted value into the runner's environment while the job is actually running, and automatically masks the values in any log output so even if a step accidentally echoes a secret, it shows up redacted. On the dbt side, profiles.yml itself is safe to commit because it doesn't contain literal values — it just references env_var('SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD') and so on, and those environment variables get populated from the GitHub Secrets at workflow runtime. The last piece I'd make sure is configured is a branch protection rule that marks this workflow as a required status check — without that, the workflow running is just informational, and people could still merge a PR with failing tests; the required check is what actually blocks the merge button until it's green.
questions.example:
name: dbt-ci
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  dbt-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      DBT_ENV_SECRET_SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT }}
      DBT_ENV_SECRET_SNOWFLAKE_USER: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_USER }}
      DBT_ENV_SECRET_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD }}
      DBT_ENV_SECRET_SNOWFLAKE_WAREHOUSE: ${{ secrets.SNOWFLAKE_WAREHOUSE }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'
      - run: pip install dbt-snowflake
      - run: dbt build --target ci
      - run: dbt test --target ci
# Branch protection: require this workflow as a status check before merge.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding credentials directly in the workflow YAML instead of referencing GitHub Secrets
Committing a profiles.yml with literal credential values instead of env_var() references
Forgetting to configure a required status check in branch protection, leaving the tests as merely informational
Running the workflow on 'push' to main only, missing the pre-merge PR gate entirely
Not scoping secrets appropriately (e.g., exposing organization-wide secrets to forked-repo PRs, which GitHub Actions restricts by default but is often misunderstood)
keyPoints: Workflow triggers on pull_request so checks run before merge
Credentials are stored as encrypted GitHub Secrets, injected only into the runner's environment at execution time
profiles.yml references env_var() rather than literal values, keeping it safe to commit
Secrets are masked in logs and never exposed in the workflow file or diffs
A required branch protection status check is what actually blocks merging on failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct pull_request trigger and dbt build/test steps
Correct use of GitHub Secrets for credentials, never hardcoded
Explains profiles.yml env_var() pattern keeping the file safe to commit
Mentions required branch protection status check to enforce the gate
Valid, runnable YAML

questions.title: Dynamic Array Formula for a Ranked Top-N With Ties
questions.prompt: You have a table of SalesReps and their TotalSales in columns A and B (with a header row). Using modern dynamic array functions, write a single formula that returns the names of the top 5 sales reps by TotalSales, sorted descending, spilling into a range automatically, without using a helper column.
questions.modelAnswer: This can be solved with a single formula combining SORT and INDEX, or more elegantly, nesting SORT with TAKE: sort the SalesReps range by TotalSales descending, then take the first 5 rows of the sorted result. Using SORT(A2:B100, 2, -1) sorts the full two-column range by the second column (TotalSales) in descending order, and wrapping that in TAKE(..., 5) extracts just the first 5 rows of the sorted array, spilling both the rep names and their totals as a single dynamic array formula — entered once, with no helper columns, and automatically recalculating and re-spilling if the underlying data changes size. If you only want the names (not totals) spilled, you can apply INDEX/CHOOSECOL on the sorted result, or more directly sort only column A using column B as the sort key via SORTBY, then TAKE the first 5: TAKE(SORTBY(A2:A100, B2:B100, -1), 5).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for SORTBY combined with TAKE here, since that avoids needing to sort the full two-column block if I only want names back. SORTBY lets me sort the SalesReps names using TotalSales as the sort key in descending order, without needing TotalSales to be adjacent or even included in the output — so SORTBY of the names range, by the TotalSales range, descending, gives me every rep sorted top to bottom by sales. Then I just wrap that in TAKE and ask for the first 5, and because both of these are dynamic array functions, the whole thing spills automatically into five cells with one formula, no helper column, and it'll keep itself correct if the underlying data grows or shrinks. If I wanted both the name and the total showing together, I'd use SORT on the full two-column range by the second column descending and then TAKE the first 5 rows of that instead.
commonMistakes: Using a helper column with RANK() and then filtering, when a single dynamic array formula is requested
Forgetting the sort order argument (-1 for descending) and getting the bottom 5 instead of top 5
Using LARGE() with INDEX/MATCH, which breaks down when there are tied TotalSales values
Hardcoding the range size instead of letting it reference the full data range (or a table/spill range) for robustness
Confusing SORT's column index argument with SORTBY's separate sort-key-array argument
keyPoints: SORTBY sorts one range using a separate range as the sort key, without requiring adjacency
TAKE extracts a fixed number of rows/columns from the front of an array result
Nesting TAKE around SORT/SORTBY produces a single spilling dynamic array formula
Descending order requires the -1 sort order argument
No helper columns are needed because the functions compose directly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct use of SORT or SORTBY with descending order
Correct use of TAKE to limit to top 5
Formula spills as a single dynamic array without helper columns
Clear explanation of why this approach is robust to data size changes
Valid Excel formula syntax

questions.title: Fix the Power Automate Flow's Silent Failures
questions.prompt: A Power Automate flow approves expense reports: it calls an HTTP action to validate the report against a finance API, then sends an approval request, then writes the result to a SharePoint list. Lately, whenever the HTTP validation call fails, the flow still proceeds to send the approval request with invalid data, and nobody is notified of the failure. Describe exactly how you'd reconfigure the flow's error handling using Run After settings to stop this, and route failures to a notification step.
questions.modelAnswer: By default, every action in Power Automate is configured with Run After set only to 'is successful' on its immediate predecessor, so on the surface the flow should already stop on HTTP failure — the actual bug described (proceeding despite a failed validation call) usually means the HTTP action's Run After configuration on the downstream approval step has been broadened, intentionally or accidentally, to include 'has failed,' 'is skipped,' or 'has timed out' in addition to 'is successful,' which causes the approval step to run regardless of the validation outcome. The fix is to open the Run After settings on the 'Send approval request' action and ensure it is configured to run only when the HTTP validation action 'has succeeded' — removing any other checked conditions. Separately, to add explicit failure notification, you add a parallel branch (or a second action attached to the same HTTP action) whose Run After is configured for 'has failed' (and optionally 'has timed out'), and that branch's action sends a Teams/email notification describing the failure, effectively implementing a try/catch pattern where the 'try' path only proceeds on success and the 'catch' path only fires on failure, both hanging off the same HTTP action. This way, a failed validation call either halts the flow before the approval request goes out, or at minimum guarantees a human is notified immediately rather than the invalid data silently proceeding through to SharePoint.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way Power Automate handles this is through each action's Run After settings, and the symptom you're describing — approval going out even when validation fails — almost always means Run After on that downstream approval action has been checked for more than just 'is successful.' If someone checked 'has failed' or 'is skipped' alongside 'is successful' on that connection, the approval step will fire no matter what happened upstream, which is exactly the bug. So step one is going into the approval action's Run After configuration and making sure only 'is successful' is checked against the HTTP validation action — that alone stops the flow from silently continuing on bad data. Step two, for the notification gap, I'd build what's essentially a try/catch pattern using the same mechanism — add a separate branch coming off that same HTTP action, but this time configure its Run After to trigger specifically on 'has failed' (and I'd usually include 'has timed out' too), and have that branch just be a Teams or email notification to whoever owns this process. So now you've got two paths hanging off the same HTTP call: the happy path only runs on success and continues to approval, and the failure path only runs on failure and notifies someone immediately — nothing falls through the cracks silently anymore.

Only fixing the approval step's Run After without adding an explicit failure-notification branch
Forgetting to also handle 'has timed out' as a failure condition, not just 'has failed'
Putting the notification action in the main success path instead of a separate Run After-configured failure branch
Not testing the fix by deliberately forcing the HTTP action to fail and confirming both that approval is blocked and the notification fires
keyPoints: Run After settings per action control which upstream outcomes (success/failure/skipped/timeout) allow it to execute
The bug is almost always an overly broad Run After configuration on the downstream action
Fix: restrict the approval action's Run After to only 'is successful'
Add a parallel failure-notification branch configured to Run After 'has failed' (and typically 'has timed out')
This creates a try/catch-equivalent pattern using two branches off the same action

Correct fix for restricting the approval step's Run After

questions.title: Python Script Visual to Clean Messy Survey Data in Power BI
questions.prompt: A dataset loaded into Power BI has a FeedbackScore column imported from a survey tool that mixes numeric strings, stray text like 'N/A', and some values with trailing whitespace or a percent sign. Write a Python script (as used in a Power BI Python script visual or Power Query Python step) using pandas that cleans this column into a proper numeric type, and explain what constraints Power BI's Python integration puts on how this script can be written.
questions.modelAnswer: The cleaning logic needs to handle three failure modes in the FeedbackScore column: trailing/leading whitespace, a trailing percent sign that needs stripping before numeric conversion, and non-numeric placeholder text like 'N/A' that should become a missing value rather than crash the conversion. Using pandas, the approach is to first coerce the column to string type and strip whitespace, then strip a trailing '%' character if present, and finally use pd.to_numeric with errors='coerce' so any value that still can't be parsed (like leftover 'N/A' text) becomes NaN instead of raising an exception that would halt the whole script. Within Power BI specifically, Python integration (both in Power Query's Run Python Script step and in a Python visual) runs in a constrained, sandboxed environment tied to a local Python installation registered in Power BI Desktop's options, has no internet access from the script, must read its input from a pre-defined dataset variable (dataset in Python visuals, or the input dataframe passed into a Power Query Python step) and must leave its output in a specifically named variable Power BI expects (e.g., a dataframe named dataset for a Python visual, or the final returned dataframe for Power Query), and critically, for the Power BI Service to refresh a dataset that uses a Python step, a Personal Gateway or equivalent gateway with the exact same Python environment installed is required, since the cloud Service itself cannot execute arbitrary Python.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd handle the cleaning in three passes with pandas. First, force the column to string and strip any leading or trailing whitespace, because that's often invisible in the raw export and silently breaks numeric parsing. Second, strip off a trailing percent sign if it's there, since that character alone will make pd.to_numeric fail even on an otherwise valid number. Third, run it through pd.to_numeric with errors='coerce' — that's the key piece, because it means anything that still isn't a valid number after the cleanup, like a stray 'N/A', just becomes NaN instead of throwing an exception and killing the whole script. On the Power BI side, there are some real constraints I'd flag to whoever's maintaining this. The Python runs locally against whatever Python environment is registered in Power BI Desktop's options — it's not running in the cloud, so there's no internet access and no arbitrary package installs happening at refresh time, only what's already installed in that environment. The script has to follow Power BI's specific input/output contract — a Python visual reads from a variable called dataset and a Power Query Python step has its own expected return shape — so you can't just write a free-form script, it has to plug into that interface. And probably the biggest operational gotcha: if this needs to refresh from the Power BI Service rather than just Desktop, you need a gateway — either a personal gateway or an on-premises data gateway — with that exact same Python environment and packages installed, because the cloud Service has no ability to execute Python itself.
questions.example:
import pandas as pd

# 'dataset' is the input dataframe provided by Power BI
df = dataset.copy()

df['FeedbackScore'] = (
    df['FeedbackScore']
    .astype(str)
    .str.strip()
    .str.rstrip('%')
)

df['FeedbackScore'] = pd.to_numeric(df['FeedbackScore'], errors='coerce')

dataset = df  # Power BI reads the cleaned result back from 'dataset'

Assuming the Python script can access the internet or install packages at Power BI Service refresh time
Forgetting that Service-side refresh of a Python step requires a gateway with a matching Python environment installed

errors='coerce' converts unparseable values to NaN instead of raising an exception
