questions.title: Fixing a SQL-Injectable Dynamic Search Procedure
questions.prompt: A teammate wrote the stored procedure below to let a reporting UI search products by color with a user-selectable sort column. Identify every injection vector in it, then rewrite it safely. Explain specifically why the color value and the sort column name have to be handled differently -- one can be parameterized directly, the other cannot.
questions.modelAnswer:
There are two separate injection vectors here, and they need two different fixes.

The first is @Color: it's concatenated directly into the string inside quotes, so a value like `Red'; DROP TABLE Production.Product; --` gets executed as part of the statement. This is the classic case sp_executesql exists to solve -- @Color is a data value, so it belongs in sp_executesql's parameter list, where SQL Server treats it strictly as data and never as executable text, no matter what characters it contains.

The second is @SortColumn, and it's actually the more dangerous one because it can't be fixed the same way. sp_executesql's parameters only substitute values -- they cannot substitute an identifier like a column name, because `ORDER BY @Param` isn't valid T-SQL (SQL Server would try to sort by a constant, not by a column). That means @SortColumn has to be handled by validation, not parameterization: either whitelist it against a known, fixed list of legal column names before it ever reaches the dynamic string, or at minimum wrap it in QUOTENAME() to neutralize bracket-based injection tricks -- and I'd do both, since QUOTENAME alone doesn't stop someone passing a syntactically valid but unintended column name.

The corrected version below parameterizes @Color through sp_executesql and validates @SortColumn against an explicit allow-list before concatenating it (safely, as an identifier, not a value).
questions.professionalAnswer:
Looking at this procedure, I'd flag it immediately in a code review -- it's building the entire WHERE and ORDER BY clause by gluing strings together, and that's a textbook SQL injection hole. There are actually two different problems stacked on top of each other, and I'd want to be clear they need different fixes. The Color value is a data value, so the right move is sp_executesql with a proper parameter -- that's the whole reason sp_executesql exists, it treats whatever gets passed in purely as data, so even something like a stray apostrophe or an embedded DROP TABLE just becomes a literal string being compared, not code getting executed.

The sort column is trickier, and I'd explain why it can't get the same treatment: you physically cannot parameterize an identifier the way you parameterize a value -- ORDER BY @SomeParam just doesn't do what you'd want, it won't sort by a column, it'll try to sort by whatever that one value is. So for something like a sort column, I always reach for a whitelist -- check the incoming value against the small, fixed list of columns we actually allow sorting by, fall back to a safe default if it's not on the list, and only then build it into the dynamic SQL as an identifier, wrapped in QUOTENAME for good measure.
commonMistakes: Parameterizing only the value and missing that the sort column is a second, separate injection vector
Trying to pass the sort column as an sp_executesql parameter, which doesn't work for identifiers
Relying on QUOTENAME alone for the sort column without an allow-list behind it
Using EXEC() with concatenated strings instead of sp_executesql
Assuming input validation on the UI side is sufficient and skipping server-side protection
keyPoints: sp_executesql parameterizes data values safely; EXEC() with concatenation does not
Identifiers (column/table names) cannot be parameterized -- only values can
Dynamic identifiers must be validated against a whitelist, optionally plus QUOTENAME
Reach for dynamic SQL only when a real identifier or structural element must vary at runtime
SQL injection risk exists even inside stored procedures, not just at the application layer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies both injection vectors (value and identifier)
Explains why sp_executesql parameters can't substitute identifiers
Provides a correct, safe rewrite using sp_executesql
Includes identifier whitelisting/QUOTENAME for the sort column
Clear overall explanation of the fix

questions.title: Diagnosing a Recurring Deadlock Between Two Order-Processing Procedures
questions.prompt: Two stored procedures are both involved in order processing: usp_UpdateOrderStatus updates the Orders table first, then OrderDetails; usp_ApplyDiscount updates OrderDetails first, then Orders. Under heavy load during a sale event, both start failing intermittently with error 1205. Walk through how you'd confirm this is a genuine deadlock rather than ordinary blocking, what SQL Server already did automatically before you even got paged, how you'd capture the diagnostic evidence, and how you'd redesign the two procedures so this stops recurring.
questions.modelAnswer:
Error 1205 is the giveaway on its own -- it's SQL Server's specific "transaction was deadlocked" error, distinct from ordinary blocking (which doesn't raise an error at all; it just makes the waiting session sit there until the lock is released or the query times out). So the first confirmation is simply that message text and code, not a guess.

Before anyone got paged, SQL Server's lock monitor already detected the cycle automatically and picked one of the two transactions as the deadlock victim, rolling it back on its own and raising 1205 in that session, while letting the other transaction proceed normally. That's expected, automatic behavior -- the problem isn't that SQL Server handled a deadlock; it's that the application design is creating deadlocks in the first place.

To get real evidence instead of guessing, I'd capture the actual deadlock graph: either the system_health Extended Events session (which captures deadlock graphs by default on every modern SQL Server instance with zero setup), or trace flag 1222 writing deadlock graphs to the error log, or a live SQL Server Profiler trace with the Deadlock graph event if I need to reproduce it under controlled load. The graph shows exactly which two sessions were involved, which resources (specific rows/keys/pages) each one held and was waiting on, and which queries were running -- that's what turns "it deadlocks sometimes" into "usp_UpdateOrderStatus held a lock on Orders row X while waiting on OrderDetails row Y, and usp_ApplyDiscount had the exact opposite."

The root cause here is visible just from the procedure descriptions, independent of the graph: the two procedures touch the same two tables in opposite order. usp_UpdateOrderStatus locks Orders then OrderDetails; usp_ApplyDiscount locks OrderDetails then Orders. Under enough concurrent load, it's inevitable that one session grabs the first lock each procedure needs right as the other grabs the second, and neither can proceed. The fix is to enforce a single, consistent access order across every procedure that touches both tables -- rewrite usp_ApplyDiscount to update Orders before OrderDetails, matching usp_UpdateOrderStatus. I'd also shorten both transactions to only what genuinely needs to be atomic, consider whether the default isolation level is adding unnecessary lock duration for this workload, and add application-side retry logic that catches 1205 specifically and retries the transaction once, since even with consistent ordering, some contention under extreme load is still possible.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd point to is that error 1205 is specific -- it's SQL Server's deadlock error, not generic blocking, so I already know what category of problem this is before I even look at the code. And something people sometimes miss: by the time I'm looking at this, SQL Server has already handled the immediate crisis on its own -- it detected the cycle, picked a victim, rolled that one transaction back, and let the other one finish. So I'm not firefighting an active deadlock; I'm investigating why this keeps happening.

To get real evidence I'd go straight to the deadlock graph -- these days that's usually just querying the system_health Extended Events session, since it captures deadlock graphs automatically without me having to turn anything on ahead of time. If I needed something more targeted I'd reach for trace flag 1222 or a Profiler trace with the deadlock graph event. That graph tells me exactly which resources each session was holding and waiting on, which is the proof, not just a theory.

But honestly, in this specific case, I could probably guess the root cause just from the procedure descriptions: one updates Orders then OrderDetails, the other does it backwards. That's the single most common cause of a deadlock -- two pieces of code locking the same two tables in opposite order. My fix is to make every procedure that touches both tables agree on one consistent order, keep the transactions as short as possible so the window for collision is small, and add retry logic around 1205 specifically on the application side as a safety net, since consistent ordering reduces deadlocks dramatically but doesn't mathematically guarantee zero under extreme concurrency.
commonMistakes: Treating ordinary blocking and a deadlock (error 1205) as the same thing
Assuming a deadlock means SQL Server malfunctioned rather than handled an application design flaw
Guessing at the cause instead of capturing the actual deadlock graph
Fixing only the symptom (retrying) without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Wrapping the entire procedure in one long transaction instead of minimizing what's actually atomic
keyPoints: Error 1205 specifically identifies a deadlock, distinct from ordinary blocking
SQL Server automatically detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen victim
system_health Extended Events / trace flag 1222 / Profiler capture the deadlock graph for real evidence
Root cause here is inconsistent table access order across the two procedures
Fix: enforce consistent access order, keep transactions short, add retry logic for 1205

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes deadlock (1205) from ordinary blocking
Describes SQL Server's automatic deadlock detection and victim rollback
Names a real diagnostic method for capturing the deadlock graph
Identifies inconsistent access order as the root cause
Proposes a concrete redesign (consistent order, shorter transactions, retry logic)
Clear, structured troubleshooting narrative

questions.title: A Nightly Staging Query's Runtime Quietly Tripled
questions.prompt: A nightly ETL step that filters Sales.SalesOrderHeader by a date range used to finish in under a minute. After a recent, unrelated application release, it now takes over 20 minutes most nights, even though nobody touched the query text itself. Walk through your full diagnostic process, in the order you'd actually do it, to find the real cause and prove your fix worked.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd work outward from the query itself before looking anywhere else, because the fact that nobody touched this query's text doesn't mean nothing that affects it changed.

First, I'd turn on the actual execution plan (Ctrl+M) and run it, looking specifically for whether an operation that used to be an Index Seek is now a Scan -- that's the single most common visible signature of a regressed query. I'd also compare estimated vs. actual row counts on each operator; a big gap there points at stale statistics giving the optimizer bad cardinality estimates, which can push it toward a much worse plan even though the query text is identical.

Second, I'd capture SET STATISTICS TIME and SET STATISTICS IO output and compare it mentally against what I'd expect for this table's size. If CPU time and elapsed time are close, it's genuinely doing more logical work; if elapsed time is much higher than CPU time, something else -- blocking, waits, disk I/O contention -- is adding wait time on top of comparable actual work, and I'd pivot to sys.dm_exec_requests / sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks to see what wait type is dominating.

Third, I'd specifically check whether the query's WHERE clause is still SARGable the way it was before. The "unrelated application release" detail is a flag: if the application layer changed how it passes the date parameter -- say, switching from a DATETIME parameter to a string that now gets implicitly converted, or wrapping the column in a function somewhere upstream that got introduced in the release -- that alone can silently turn a seek into a scan without anyone touching this specific query's text.

Fourth, if this runs as a parameterized query or inside a stored procedure, I'd consider parameter sniffing: if the release changed what date ranges get passed first after a recompile, SQL Server may have cached a plan optimized for a very different-sized result set than what's typically requested now. I'd check sys.dm_exec_query_stats for that procedure's cached plan and compare it against a fresh OPTION (RECOMPILE) run.

Fifth, I'd check whether an index this query relied on was changed, disabled, or had its fill factor/maintenance schedule altered as part of the release, and whether statistics were updated recently -- a large data load with no corresponding stats update is a very common, very quiet cause of exactly this symptom.

Finally, I'd correlate the actual onset against the release timeline and any index maintenance job history, form a specific hypothesis from whichever of the above turned up concrete evidence, apply the fix (rebuild/update statistics, restore a missing index, fix an implicit conversion, add OPTION (RECOMPILE) or a plan guide for parameter sniffing), and then prove it with a direct before/after comparison of logical reads via SET STATISTICS IO -- that number is the most reliable proof a fix genuinely reduced work, independent of how busy the server happened to be at the moment I measured it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't jump straight to 'rebuild the index' or 'update stats' -- I'd want to actually see what changed first. So step one for me is always the actual execution plan, Ctrl+M, run the query, and look specifically for a scan where I'd expect a seek, plus a big gap between estimated and actual row counts, because that gap is basically SQL Server telling you its statistics are lying to it.

Step two, I'd pull SET STATISTICS TIME and IO and look at whether CPU time and elapsed time line up. If they're close, the engine's genuinely doing more work. If elapsed time is way bigger than CPU time, I know to go look at waits and blocking instead of the query logic itself.

The detail that really jumps out at me in this scenario is 'an unrelated application release' right before this started. That's exactly the kind of thing that quietly breaks SARGability without anyone touching the SQL -- maybe the app now sends the date as a string instead of a proper date, and now there's an implicit conversion happening on every row. I'd check that specifically.

If this lives inside a stored procedure, parameter sniffing is next on my list -- the first execution after a recompile caches a plan shaped for whatever parameter came in that first time, and if the typical date range changed after the release, that cached plan might be wrong for almost every call since. And I'd double check whether an index got dropped, disabled, or just went stale from a big data load with no corresponding stats update around the same time as the release.

Whatever I land on, I don't call it fixed until I've got a before-and-after comparison of logical reads from STATISTICS IO -- that number doesn't lie the way timing can when the server's under different load each time I test.
commonMistakes: Assuming the query must be unchanged and therefore can't be the cause
Jumping to 'rebuild all the indexes' without first checking the actual plan for a scan-vs-seek regression
Ignoring that an unrelated application change can break SARGability through implicit conversion
Not checking for parameter sniffing on parameterized/stored-procedure queries
Declaring victory based on a single wall-clock timing instead of logical reads before/after
keyPoints: Start with the actual execution plan: look for scan-vs-seek regressions and estimated/actual row count gaps
SET STATISTICS TIME/IO separates CPU-bound work from waiting/blocking
An unrelated release can break SARGability via implicit conversion or a changed parameter type
Parameter sniffing is a real suspect for parameterized/stored-procedure queries after a recompile
Check for dropped/disabled indexes and stale statistics correlated with the release timeline
Prove the fix with a before/after logical-reads comparison, not just a timing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Starts diagnosis with the actual execution plan
Uses STATISTICS TIME/IO to separate CPU vs. wait-driven slowness
Considers SARGability/implicit conversion broken by the unrelated release
Considers parameter sniffing as a plausible cause
Checks indexing/statistics changes correlated with the release
Proves the fix with evidence (logical reads before/after)

questions.title: Diagnosing Unexpected Totals From CALCULATE Inside SUMX
questions.prompt: A measure written as CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), FILTER(Customer, [Customer Measure] > 100)), where [Customer Measure] itself calls CALCULATE on Sales, returns totals that shift unexpectedly when a product-category slicer is applied - numbers that don't match a hand-calculated expectation. Walk through how you'd diagnose the context-transition behavior causing this.
questions.modelAnswer: The core thing to check is what happens to [Customer Measure] inside that FILTER. FILTER(Customer, ...) iterates the Customer table row by row - that's row context. [Customer Measure] is a measure reference, and every measure reference is implicitly wrapped in its own CALCULATE, which means context transition fires for every single customer row: the current customer's row context gets converted into a one-customer filter context before [Customer Measure] evaluates. Critically, that implicit CALCULATE also inherits whatever filter context is already active outside, including the product-category slicer. So [Customer Measure] isn't being evaluated against 'this customer, all products' per row; it's being evaluated against 'this customer, intersected with whatever category the slicer currently has selected.' That's almost certainly the source of the shifting numbers: as the slicer changes, the per-row result of [Customer Measure] changes for every customer, which changes which customers pass the >100 threshold inside FILTER, which changes the set of customers the outer SUM runs against - a compounding effect, not a simple scaling. To diagnose concretely: temporarily rewrite [Customer Measure] as a plain CALCULATE expression inline so the context transition is visible instead of hidden behind a measure reference; use a VAR to capture [Customer Measure]'s value for one specific, known customer under two different slicer selections and compare them directly - if they differ, that confirms the slicer is reaching into the per-row evaluation via context transition, which is expected behavior, not a bug; then decide whether that's actually wanted - if the threshold should be evaluated against each customer's all-time total regardless of the slicer, wrap the inner measure's CALCULATE with ALL(Product) or REMOVEFILTERS(Product) to deliberately cut it off from the slicer, rather than letting it inherit by default.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd zero in on is that FILTER(Customer, [Customer Measure] > 100) is evaluating [Customer Measure] once per customer row, and since that's a measure reference sitting inside row context, it's implicitly wrapped in its own CALCULATE - so context transition fires for every row, and that implicit CALCULATE picks up whatever filter context is already active, including the category slicer. So the per-customer threshold check isn't really 'does this customer's all-time value exceed 100,' it's 'does this customer's value under the currently selected category exceed 100' - and that set of qualifying customers shifts every time the slicer changes, which compounds into the outer SUM. To prove that's what's happening, I'd isolate one known customer with a VAR, evaluate [Customer Measure] for them under two different slicer states, and compare the numbers directly - if they differ, that confirms the slicer is reaching inside the per-row evaluation. Then it's a design decision: if the threshold is supposed to ignore the slicer, I'd wrap the inner measure's CALCULATE with ALL or REMOVEFILTERS on the category column so it stops inheriting that context.
questions.example: Debug step: VAR TestCustomerValue = CALCULATE([Customer Measure], Customer[CustomerKey] = 123) RETURN TestCustomerValue - evaluated once with the category slicer set to 'Bikes' and once cleared, to see directly whether the per-customer value is slicer-dependent.
commonMistakes: Assuming a measure reference inside FILTER behaves like a plain column and ignores outer filter context
Not realizing context transition means the implicit CALCULATE inherits the active filter context, including slicers
Treating the shifting totals as a bug instead of correct (if unintended) behavior that needs a deliberate ALL/REMOVEFILTERS fix
Debugging by staring at the final number instead of isolating one row's value with a VAR
keyPoints: Measure references inside row context trigger implicit CALCULATE / context transition
Context transition inherits the currently active filter context, including slicers, unless explicitly overridden
FILTER iterating a table creates row context for every measure called inside it
Isolate one row's value with VAR under different filter states to confirm the behavior
Use ALL/REMOVEFILTERS inside the inner measure if the threshold should ignore the slicer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains implicit CALCULATE/context transition inside FILTER
Explains why the slicer reaches into the per-row evaluation
Proposes a concrete isolation/debugging technique
Proposes a correct fix (ALL/REMOVEFILTERS) if slicer independence is desired

questions.title: A Percent-of-Total Measure Ignores the Slicer
questions.prompt: A '% of Total' measure was built as DIVIDE([Sales], CALCULATE([Sales], ALL(Sales))). Stakeholders report that when they select a single region in a slicer, the percentages across the visible categories don't sum to 100% - they're much smaller than expected. Diagnose the cause and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: This is working exactly as ALL is defined to work - the symptom isn't a bug, it's a mismatch between what the measure computes and what the stakeholders actually want. ALL(Sales) clears every filter on Sales unconditionally, including the region slicer, so the denominator is always the worldwide total across every region, every time, no matter what's selected. When a user filters to one region, the numerator shrinks to that region's sales but the denominator stays at the full worldwide total - so the percentages correctly reflect 'this category's share of everyone, everywhere,' which only sums to 100% when nothing is filtered, and sums to something much smaller once a region is selected, exactly as reported. What the stakeholders actually want is a visual total: a percentage of what's currently selected, the one region, not of the whole dataset. That's ALLSELECTED's job specifically - it keeps the filters applied outside the visual, the region slicer, and only clears the breakdown generated by the visual itself. Swapping ALL(Sales) for ALLSELECTED() in the denominator fixes it: the denominator becomes 'total sales for the currently selected region,' which the numerators, each category's sales within that region, correctly sum to 100% of.
questions.professionalAnswer: This isn't actually broken DAX, it's answering a different question than the one being asked. ALL(Sales) wipes out every filter on that table, the region slicer included, so no matter what someone picks, the denominator is always the full worldwide total. That's why, once you filter to one region, the numbers only add up to that region's small slice of the world instead of 100% - the math is doing exactly what ALL tells it to do. What the stakeholders actually want is for the denominator to respect their region selection and only ignore the category breakdown the visual itself creates - that's precisely what ALLSELECTED does. Swapping ALL(Sales) for ALLSELECTED() in the denominator means the total becomes 'everything selected, in this case the one region,' and the category percentages go back to summing to 100% of that.
questions.example: Before the fix, selecting 'West' region: numerator = West's category sales, denominator = worldwide total, so percentages sum to roughly West's share of the world, well under 100%. After the fix: denominator = West's total, so percentages correctly sum to 100% of West.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a bug in ALL rather than the wrong function choice for the requirement
Trying to 'fix' it by adding more filter arguments to ALL instead of switching to ALLSELECTED
Not testing the measure with a slicer selection active before shipping it, so the discrepancy wasn't caught earlier
Assuming ALLSELECTED and ALL are interchangeable because they both start with 'ALL'
keyPoints: ALL clears report-level/slicer filters too, not just the visual's own breakdown
A percentage that should respect slicer selections needs ALLSELECTED, not ALL
Always test ratio/percent-of-total measures with a slicer active, not just unfiltered
The underlying DAX wasn't broken - it was answering a different question than the one asked

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses ALL as clearing the slicer filter too
Explains why percentages don't sum to 100% once filtered
Correct ALLSELECTED-based fix
Frames it as a requirement mismatch, not a DAX bug

questions.title: A Nightly Procedure That Used to Finish in Minutes Now Takes Hours
questions.prompt: A nightly stored procedure that updates loyalty points for every customer who made a purchase that day used to finish in under five minutes. Over the last two months it's crept up to three hours, and nobody changed the procedure's code. When you open it, you find it's built around a cursor that loops through qualifying customers one at a time, calling an UPDATE inside the loop. Walk through how you'd confirm the cursor is the real problem, why its cost grows disproportionately as the table grows, and how you'd rewrite it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I wouldn't assume the cursor is guilty just because cursors have a bad reputation -- I'd confirm it with SET STATISTICS TIME and IO around the existing procedure, and separately time a rewritten set-based version against the same day's data, so the comparison is based on actual numbers rather than instinct. I'd also check whether the cursor's own underlying SELECT has degraded (stale statistics causing a scan instead of a seek on the qualifying-customers query), since that's a second, compounding problem that's easy to miss if you only blame the loop itself.

The reason a cursor's cost grows disproportionately as a table grows isn't just that there are more rows to loop over -- it's that every iteration carries fixed per-row overhead (a context switch between the engine and the cursor machinery, its own mini-transaction and log record for each UPDATE, lock acquisition and release every single time) that a single set-based statement pays only once, not once per row. As the qualifying-customer count has grown month over month with the business, that per-row overhead has been multiplying against a growing row count, which is exactly the kind of cost curve that looks fine for a long time and then visibly takes off -- nobody changed the code, but the data volume the same code runs against did.

The rewrite replaces the entire loop with a single set-based UPDATE ... FROM that joins the same filtering logic the cursor used to decide which customers qualify, letting the engine process the whole batch as one operation instead of thousands of tiny ones.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to actually prove it's the cursor rather than just assuming it, because cursors get blamed a lot but I want real numbers. I'd run STATISTICS TIME and IO on the existing procedure, and time a rewritten set-based version against the same data, and compare. I'd also take a look at the cursor's own underlying query, because sometimes the real second problem is that it's degraded from a seek to a scan as the table's grown, on top of the cursor overhead itself. As for why this crept up without the code changing -- a cursor pays a fixed cost per row, every iteration, things like its own mini-transaction and locking overhead, and a single set-based statement only pays that cost once for the whole batch. As the number of qualifying customers has grown with the business over the last couple months, that per-row cost has been compounding against a bigger row count every single night, which is exactly the kind of thing that looks fine for a long time and then suddenly doesn't. The actual fix is just replacing the whole loop with one UPDATE statement that joins against the same qualifying criteria the cursor used, so the engine handles it as a single batch operation instead of thousands of small ones.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'nobody changed the code' rules out a regression, missing that growing data volume is itself the real cause
Not profiling with STATISTICS TIME/IO before concluding the cursor is the bottleneck
Rewriting to a WHILE loop over a temp table instead of a true single set-based statement, which is still slow
Not checking whether the cursor's underlying SELECT has also degraded due to stale statistics
keyPoints: Confirm the cause with STATISTICS TIME/IO or direct timing, not assumption
Cursor cost scales with fixed per-row overhead that compounds as row counts grow month over month
Check the cursor's own driving query for separate degradation (stale stats, scan vs. seek)
Rewrite as one set-based UPDATE ... FROM statement
Validate the rewrite produces identical results before replacing the original in production

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a concrete way to confirm the cursor is the bottleneck
Explains why cursor cost compounds as data grows
Correctly rewrites the loop as a set-based UPDATE
Addresses validation before production rollout

questions.title: Blocking Caused by a Missing Index, Not a Bug in the Code
questions.prompt: Every weekday around 10 AM, the order-entry application starts timing out for a few minutes. SQL Server's Activity Monitor shows dozens of INSERT statements from the app blocked behind a single SELECT from a management report that joins Orders to OrderLines. The report query and the INSERT statements haven't changed in months. sys.dm_tran_locks shows the report query holding a table-level (not row-level) lock on OrderLines. Diagnose why a plain SELECT is blocking INSERTs this badly, and fix it.
questions.code:
SELECT o.OrderId, ol.ProductId, ol.Quantity
FROM Orders o
JOIN OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderId = o.OrderId
WHERE o.SalesRepId = @RepId;
questions.modelAnswer:
A SELECT without an explicit hint doesn't normally take a table lock, so the first question is how that scan turned into one. With no supporting index on OrderLines for whatever predicate or join path the optimizer chose, the engine has to touch a large number of rows via a scan, taking a shared lock on each one it visits. SQL Server has a finite lock memory budget, and when the number of individual locks held by one statement crosses an internal threshold, it automatically escalates from many fine-grained row/page locks to a single table-level lock to reduce lock management overhead. That table-level shared lock is compatible with other readers but blocks writers outright, which is exactly why INSERTs into OrderLines pile up behind it even though the report is 'just reading.'

The fix starts with the execution plan: confirm there's a scan (not a seek) on OrderLines and identify which column the join or filter actually needs. If OrderLines has no index on OrderId (or on whatever column anchors the join to Orders), add a nonclustered index on that column, with included columns for ProductId and Quantity if this query is frequent enough to want a fully covering index. A seek against that index touches far fewer rows, likely staying well under the escalation threshold. If the table is simply very large and even a seek'ed range returns many rows, enabling Read Committed Snapshot Isolation removes the shared-lock-vs-insert conflict entirely for this pattern, since readers would work off row versions rather than blocking locks - though that's an instance-wide (or database-wide) behavior change that needs sign-off, not a drive-by fix. I'd pair the index fix with monitoring for LOCK_ESCALATION events going forward so this class of problem surfaces before users notice it again.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by not trusting 'nothing changed in the code' as proof nothing changed - data volume grows even when queries don't, and a join that used to be cheap can quietly cross the row-count threshold where the optimizer stops seeking and starts scanning. So first I pull the actual execution plan for that report query and check OrderLines for a scan versus a seek. If it's scanning, that tells me there's no supporting index for the join, and all those row locks it's picking up along the way are what's triggering SQL Server's automatic lock escalation to a table lock - which is the real reason a read is blocking writes so hard. My fix is almost always to add the missing index first, because a seek that only touches the rows it needs rarely escalates at all. If I add the index and it's still escalating because the table's genuinely huge and the result set is wide, then I'd bring RCSI into the conversation as a bigger architectural change, but I wouldn't reach for that first since it changes isolation behavior for everyone, not just this one report.
questions.example:
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_OrderLines_OrderId ON dbo.OrderLines (OrderId) INCLUDE (ProductId, Quantity);
-- Verify with: SET STATISTICS IO ON; and re-check the plan for an Index Seek instead of a Clustered Index Scan on OrderLines.
commonMistakes: Assuming a SELECT can't cause serious blocking, so looking everywhere except the report query itself
Jumping straight to NOLOCK hints or snapshot isolation without first checking whether a missing index is the real root cause
Not checking sys.dm_tran_locks or the execution plan to confirm an escalation actually happened versus assuming it from symptoms alone
Adding an index without included columns, fixing the seek but still causing extra key lookups under load
Treating the fix as done without monitoring for future LOCK_ESCALATION events as data grows
keyPoints: Lock escalation automatically converts many row/page locks into one table lock once a statement exceeds the lock count threshold
A missing index forcing a scan is the most common trigger for escalation on an otherwise 'simple' read
Confirm with the execution plan (scan vs seek) and sys.dm_tran_locks before proposing a fix
A targeted covering index is usually the right first fix; RCSI is a bigger, instance-level decision
Index design should include the columns actually returned, not just the join key, to avoid extra lookups

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the scan-to-lock-escalation mechanism
Identifies missing index as the likely root cause and how to confirm it
Proposes a correct, appropriately scoped index fix
Mentions RCSI as a secondary option with its tradeoffs, not a first resort
Clarity and structure of the answer

lessonLink.label: Clustered vs. Nonclustered Indexes: Choosing Wisely

questions.title: A Margin Measure That's Right on Every Row but 'Wrong' on the Grand Total
questions.prompt: A Profit Margin % measure is defined as DIVIDE([Total Profit],[Total Sales]) and shows correct, verified percentages on every product row of a table visual. Finance insists the Grand Total row is wrong, because it doesn't match what you'd get by averaging the visible row percentages. Explain what's actually happening and how you'd resolve the disagreement with Finance.
questions.code:
Profit Margin % = DIVIDE([Total Profit], [Total Sales])
Total Profit = SUM(Sales[Profit])
Total Sales = SUM(Sales[SalesAmount])
questions.modelAnswer:
The behavior Finance is flagging isn't a bug in the measure - it's expected, correct behavior for a ratio that isn't additive across the grain of the visual. At the Grand Total row, DAX re-evaluates DIVIDE([Total Profit],[Total Sales]) in the filter context of the total, which means it sums profit across all products, sums sales across all products, and divides those two aggregated totals. That is mathematically the weighted average margin across the business, weighted by each product's sales volume. A simple arithmetic average of the per-row percentages, by contrast, would give every product equal weight regardless of how much it actually sold, which is a different (and usually less meaningful) number for a margin KPI. Those two numbers will diverge whenever product-level sales volumes vary significantly, and that's exactly the situation here.

Before telling Finance 'it's working as intended,' I'd still run a sanity check to rule out an actual bug masquerading as this behavior - things like an inactive or bidirectional relationship, a slicer not applying consistently, or a stray ALLSELECTED/ALL somewhere in a related measure that would make the total ignore filters the rows respect. If the raw Total Profit and Total Sales numbers at the grand total tie out to the sum of the visible rows' underlying profit and sales (not their displayed percentages), that confirms the measure is correct and the disagreement is really about which statistic Finance wants to see. At that point I'd explain the weighted-average interpretation directly, and if they genuinely want a simple average of the displayed percentages for some other purpose, I'd build that as an explicitly separate, clearly labeled measure using AVERAGEX over the visible products rather than overwrite the correct weighted margin.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, the first thing I'd do is not panic and assume my DAX is broken, because this exact complaint comes up constantly with any kind of percentage or ratio measure. I'd explain to Finance that the total row isn't averaging the percentages they see - it's recalculating the ratio from the underlying totals, profit over sales, both summed across everything in view. That's actually the weighted average, which gives bigger products more say in the number, and it's usually the more honest number for a margin KPI than treating a tiny product and a huge product as equally important. Before I go explain that, though, I always double check the raw numbers underneath - pull Total Profit and Total Sales at the total level and confirm they really do equal the sum of what's on the rows - because I want to rule out that something like a sneaky bidirectional relationship is actually causing a real discrepancy before I confidently tell Finance 'this is correct.' If after that check it really is just the weighted-vs-simple-average distinction, I'll offer to add a separate, clearly labeled simple-average measure if that's genuinely what they want for some other view, but I wouldn't change the margin measure itself to do something mathematically less correct.
commonMistakes: Assuming the total is wrong just because it doesn't match an average of the displayed row percentages
'Fixing' it by wrapping the measure in AVERAGEX over the ratio, which silently changes the math to something less correct for a margin KPI
Not validating the raw underlying totals before concluding the behavior is expected rather than a real bug
Not recognizing that this is a filter-context re-evaluation, not a context-transition issue, and explaining it with the wrong mechanism
Failing to communicate the distinction to stakeholders in plain terms, leaving them thinking the model itself is unreliable
keyPoints: Ratio measures aren't additive - the total re-evaluates the ratio of aggregated totals, not an average of row ratios
This total represents a sales-weighted average margin, which is usually more meaningful than a simple average
Validate raw totals first to rule out an actual bug (bad relationship, stray ALL/ALLSELECTED) before concluding it's expected behavior
Offer a separate, explicitly labeled measure if stakeholders truly want the simple-average interpretation
Clear communication of 'why' is as important as the technical diagnosis here

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why the total differs from a row-average correctly
Describes concrete validation steps to rule out a real bug
Correctly characterizes the total as a weighted average and why that matters
Proposes an appropriate way to satisfy a genuine alternate requirement without breaking the measure
Clarity

questions.title: A Scatter Plot That Went From 5 Seconds to 40 After One LOD Calculation
questions.prompt: A Tableau dashboard rendered in under 5 seconds before an analyst added a FIXED-level-of-detail calculation (Customer Lifetime Value) to color 200,000 marks on a scatter plot. The data source is a live connection to a SQL Server view, and the dashboard has four interactive filters. After the change, the dashboard takes 40+ seconds to load. Diagnose the slowdown and propose fixes.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first thing I'd check is whether the LOD calculation is actually being recomputed against the live SQL Server source on every interaction, rather than cached. A FIXED LOD forces Tableau to compute an aggregation at the specified granularity (Customer ID here) as a distinct query step, and on a live connection, that step re-executes against the source essentially every time the view's query changes - including filter interactions that don't even apply to the LOD if it isn't wrapped in a context filter. With 200,000 customers and a live SQL Server view (which may itself be doing joins or calculations server-side), that FIXED aggregation query can be expensive, and it's firing far more often than the four slow-changing filters would suggest it needs to.

I'd confirm this with Tableau's Performance Recorder before changing anything, to see exactly how much time is spent in the LOD's generated query versus rendering versus other calculations. If the LOD query is the dominant cost, the most effective fix is usually converting the data source to an extract - Tableau's extract engine handles LOD calculations far more efficiently than round-tripping to a live relational source, and it removes the dependency on SQL Server's query performance entirely for this interaction pattern. If a live connection is required for other reasons, the next lever is context filters: if the four filters are meant to narrow the population the LOD is computed over, making them context filters changes the order of operations so the LOD computes only within the filtered subset rather than against the full table every time. Finally, I'd look at the SQL Server side - confirming there's a usable index on Customer ID and that the view itself isn't doing unnecessary work - since a live LOD's performance is ultimately bounded by how fast the source can answer that fixed-grain aggregation query.
questions.professionalAnswer: My instinct here isn't to blame the LOD calculation in the abstract - FIXED LODs get a bad reputation, but the real culprit is almost always the combination of FIXED plus a live connection. I'd open the Performance Recorder first and actually watch where the 40 seconds goes, because guessing wastes time. If it's dominated by the generated SQL query for that FIXED calculation, that tells me Tableau is going back to SQL Server for that aggregation far more often than it should, probably on every filter click even when the filter has nothing to do with customer-level profitability. From there my first move is almost always 'can this be an extract instead of live' - extracts are just built differently for this kind of aggregation and it usually fixes the problem outright. If live is non-negotiable, I'd look at whether those four filters should be context filters, since that changes whether the LOD recomputes against the whole table or just the already-filtered slice. And I'd still go check the SQL Server view and make sure Customer ID has a sensible index, because at 200,000 rows that shouldn't be slow on a healthy source table either.
commonMistakes: Blaming FIXED LODs generically without checking whether live-connection re-execution is the actual mechanism
Skipping the Performance Recorder and guessing at the bottleneck
Assuming the existing filters automatically narrow what the LOD computes over, without checking context filter settings
Jumping straight to rewriting the calculation as a table calc without diagnosing where the time is actually spent
Ignoring the source-side query cost (indexing, view complexity) on a live connection
keyPoints: FIXED LOD granularity determines a separate aggregation query that re-executes against a live source on many interactions
Performance Recorder should be used to confirm the bottleneck before changing anything
Converting to an extract is usually the single highest-leverage fix for this pattern
Context filters change the order of operations so the LOD computes over an already-filtered set
Source-side indexing/view design still matters for live-connection LOD performance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains FIXED LOD + live connection re-execution mechanism
Uses or mentions Performance Recorder as the diagnostic step
Proposes extract conversion and/or context filters as concrete fixes
Addresses source-side (SQL Server) performance considerations
Clarity

questions.title: A Pipeline That Fails on Two Nights Out of Seven, With No Retry Policy
questions.prompt: A nightly Data Factory pipeline copies data from an on-premises SQL Server to Azure Data Lake using a self-hosted integration runtime. It fails roughly two nights out of seven with a generic 'ErrorCode=SqlOperationFailed, Code=121, Timeout expired' message. There is no retry policy configured on the Copy activity. A manual rerun the next morning always succeeds. Describe how you'd investigate this and what you'd fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
A generic SQL timeout on an intermittent schedule points me toward resource contention or network conditions rather than a logic bug, since the same pipeline and query succeed cleanly most nights and always on manual rerun. I'd start in the Monitor hub to confirm exactly which activity failed and its duration right up to the timeout, then check the self-hosted integration runtime's node health (CPU, memory, available connections) around the failure window, since a single-node self-hosted IR is a shared resource that can be starved by other on-premises activity - most commonly overlapping backup jobs, index maintenance windows, or other batch processes that happen to run at a similar time but not every night. I'd also check whether the source query itself does a large, unfiltered scan that depends on how much data has accumulated, since a slow night might simply be a night where the extract had more rows to move or the source server was mid-maintenance.

Once I understand the pattern, I'd apply two layers of fix. First, a basic safety net: add a retry policy on the Copy activity with a sensible interval and increase the command timeout, since 'fails twice a week, succeeds on manual rerun' is exactly the signature a modest retry policy is meant to catch automatically instead of requiring someone to notice and intervene by morning. Second, the actual root-cause fix: if it's resource contention from a single self-hosted IR node, I'd look at scaling to a second node for high availability and load distribution, or rescheduling the pipeline to avoid the overlapping on-prem maintenance window entirely. I'd also set up alerting on pipeline failure so this gets caught the same night rather than discovered by a user the next day, and log activity-level metrics to Log Analytics so the next intermittent issue has a historical pattern to compare against immediately.
questions.professionalAnswer: Intermittent plus 'works fine on manual rerun' is basically the classic signature of a resource or environment problem, not a code problem, so I wouldn't spend much time re-reading the pipeline logic itself. I'd go straight to the Monitor hub to nail down exactly which activity and how long it ran before timing out, and then I'd check the self-hosted IR's node health for those specific nights - CPU, memory, whatever else was running on that box around the same time. In my experience it's almost always something else on-prem competing for resources, like a backup window that doesn't run every single night. While I'm there I'd also just add a retry policy on the Copy activity, because honestly there's no excuse for not having one on an unattended nightly job - that alone would probably make this stop being a human-noticed problem even before I find the deeper cause. Longer term, if it really is IR resource contention, I'd push for a second IR node for redundancy and look at shifting the schedule a bit so it's not fighting with whatever else is hogging that server.
commonMistakes: Assuming it's a pipeline logic bug and re-reviewing the Copy activity configuration instead of checking IR and source-server resource health
Not adding a retry policy as a basic safety net, leaving an unattended nightly job with zero resilience to transient failures
Not checking for concurrent on-premises jobs (backups, maintenance) that could explain the intermittent pattern
Treating 'manual rerun works' as proof the problem is solved rather than evidence pointing toward a timing/resource issue
Not considering single self-hosted IR node as a single point of failure/bottleneck
keyPoints: Intermittent failure plus successful manual rerun points to resource contention or timing, not pipeline logic
Check self-hosted IR node health and concurrent on-premises jobs around the failure window
Add a retry policy and increase command timeout as an immediate safety net
Consider scaling the self-hosted IR to multiple nodes for both capacity and high availability
Set up alerting and centralized logging so intermittent issues are caught the same night

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons toward resource/timing contention rather than a code bug
Describes concrete diagnostic steps (Monitor hub, IR node health, concurrent jobs)
Proposes retry policy and timeout tuning as immediate mitigation
Proposes IR scaling/HA or scheduling fix as the deeper remedy
Clarity

questions.title: Dynamic RLS Works in 'View As Roles' but Not for Real Users
questions.prompt: You've configured dynamic Row-Level Security in a Power BI semantic model so regional managers see only their own region, using USERPRINCIPALNAME() looked up against a UserRegion mapping table. Testing with 'View as Roles' in Desktop filters correctly for every region. After publishing, several real regional managers report they can see every region's data once logged into the Service. Diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer:
'View as Roles' in Desktop only simulates the DAX filter logic itself - it never exercises the parts of RLS enforcement that only exist in the Service, which is exactly where I'd look first. The single most common cause of 'RLS works in testing but not for real users' is that those specific users hold a workspace role of Admin, Member, or Contributor rather than Viewer (or app access without an elevated workspace role) - RLS is enforced only for Viewer-level access and for apps/shared content, and anyone with edit-level workspace permissions bypasses it entirely by design, since they're expected to be able to see the underlying data to build and maintain content. The second thing I'd check is whether the roles were actually assigned to the affected users or their security groups under the dataset's Security settings in the Service - defining a role in Desktop does nothing in the Service until someone explicitly assigns members to it there, and that assignment step is easy to miss or to apply only to some users during rollout.

If both of those check out, I'd check for case-sensitivity or formatting mismatches between USERPRINCIPALNAME() and the Email column in UserRegionMap - trailing whitespace, differing casing conventions, or an email alias versus UPN mismatch will make LOOKUPVALUE return blank, and depending on how the rest of the model handles a blank region, that can silently resolve to 'no filter applied' rather than an error. Finally, I'd check whether any of the affected users are intentionally or accidentally members of more than one role; Power BI unions (ORs) the filters from every role a user belongs to, so if a user is in both 'Regional - West' and some broader role like 'Global Readonly' that doesn't filter by region at all, they'll see everything, which looks identical to RLS 'not working' but is actually RLS working exactly as configured.
questions.professionalAnswer: Whenever I hear 'it worked in View as Roles but not for real users,' my first question is always about workspace permissions, because that's the gap nobody remembers until they hit it: RLS simply doesn't apply to anyone with Admin, Member, or Contributor access to the workspace - only Viewers and app consumers get filtered. So I'd check what role those specific managers actually have on the workspace before I touch the DAX at all. If they're genuinely Viewers, then I'd go check the Security settings on the published dataset in the Service, because defining roles in Desktop is only half the job - you have to go assign actual users or groups to those roles after publishing, and that step gets skipped surprisingly often during a rollout. After that I'd sanity-check the USERPRINCIPALNAME-to-email matching for case or whitespace issues, and I'd specifically check whether any of these users are sitting in more than one role, since Power BI doesn't intersect multiple roles' filters, it unions them - so being in a second, broader role can silently cancel out the regional restriction even though the regional role itself is configured correctly.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that workspace Admin, Member, and Contributor roles bypass RLS entirely, regardless of role assignment
Assuming defining roles in Desktop automatically applies them in the Service without explicit role assignment under dataset Security
Not checking for case/whitespace mismatches between USERPRINCIPALNAME() and the mapping table's email column
Not recognizing that membership in multiple roles unions (not intersects) the resulting access
Treating 'View as Roles' success in Desktop as proof the Service behavior will be identical
keyPoints: RLS is enforced only for Viewer-level/app access, not for Admin, Member, or Contributor workspace roles
Roles must be explicitly assigned to users or groups under the dataset's Security settings in the Service
USERPRINCIPALNAME() matching issues (case, whitespace, alias vs UPN) can silently produce no filter
Multiple role membership unions permissions rather than intersecting them
Desktop's 'View as Roles' doesn't exercise Service-only enforcement gaps

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies workspace-role bypass as the primary likely cause
Identifies missing role assignment in Service Security settings
Explains multi-role union behavior correctly
Mentions USERPRINCIPALNAME matching issues as a secondary check
Clarity

questions.title: dbt Tests Pass on Every Laptop but Fail Every Time in CI
questions.prompt: A dbt model's unique and not_null tests on a surrogate key pass consistently on every developer's machine, but fail every single time in the GitHub Actions CI job with duplicate-key violations. CI runs 'dbt build' against a dedicated schema that's rebuilt from scratch each run. What's your diagnostic process, and what's the most likely root cause?
questions.modelAnswer:
The detail that jumps out is 'rebuilt from scratch each run,' because that forces the incremental model to run as a full-refresh in CI every time, while developers running locally against an existing dev schema are typically only ever processing new or incremental batches of data. That difference in execution path is exactly the kind of thing that can mask a surrogate-key bug on every developer machine while exposing it reliably in CI: if the surrogate key is generated from a hash of columns that aren't actually unique across the full history of the source data - commonly missing a date or batch-identifying component - small incremental batches rarely contain the colliding rows, but a full rebuild over the entire history surfaces every duplicate at once.

To confirm this, I'd reproduce it locally by running 'dbt run --full-refresh' against a scratch schema rather than trusting the incremental path, which should reproduce the same duplicate-key failures CI is seeing. Once reproduced, I'd inspect the surrogate-key generation logic (whatever columns feed the hash or generate_surrogate_key call) and find the natural-key columns that don't uniquely identify a row across the full dataset - fixing it means adding whatever column is missing from the key definition, or adding explicit deduplication logic (a ROW_NUMBER/QUALIFY pattern keeping the correct version of a duplicated natural key) before building the surrogate key. I'd also treat this as a reminder to deliberately test both full-refresh and incremental paths locally before merging changes to any incremental model, rather than assuming CI's job is simply 'flaky.'
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd zero in on immediately is that CI rebuilding the schema from scratch means it's always doing a full-refresh, while everyone's laptop is almost certainly running the incremental path against whatever's already sitting in their dev schema. That's not a CI quirk, that's CI accidentally testing a code path nobody's been exercising locally. So before I blame the pipeline, I'd run 'dbt run --full-refresh' on my own machine and see if I can reproduce the exact same duplicate-key failures - and I'd bet I can. If so, the real bug is almost certainly in how the surrogate key gets built: it's probably hashing a set of columns that look unique in a small incremental batch but aren't actually unique once you look at the full history, so the fix is adding whatever discriminating column is missing, or putting explicit dedup logic in front of the key generation. I'd also flag this as a gap in how we test locally going forward - full-refresh needs to be part of the routine check, not just something CI happens to force on us.
commonMistakes: Blaming CI as 'flaky' or environment-specific without reproducing the failure locally
Not recognizing that a schema rebuilt from scratch forces a full-refresh code path that differs from everyday incremental runs
Not testing locally with --full-refresh before assuming the bug only exists in CI
Assuming the surrogate key is unique just because it passed tests on small incremental batches
Fixing it by disabling or loosening the unique/not_null tests rather than fixing the underlying key logic
keyPoints: CI rebuilding from scratch forces a full-refresh path that differs from developers' incremental local runs
Reproduce locally with dbt run --full-refresh before assuming CI itself is the problem
Surrogate keys must be unique across the full history, not just within small incremental batches
Fix by adding the missing discriminating column to the key or adding explicit dedup logic
Treat CI's full-refresh exposure as a legitimate bug catch, not an annoyance to work around

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the full-refresh vs incremental discrepancy as the mechanism
Identifies surrogate-key uniqueness/dedup as the likely root cause
Describes a concrete local reproduction step
Proposes a correct fix (key redesign or dedup logic)
Clarity

questions.title: A Flow That 'Succeeded' but Never Actually Sent the Report
questions.prompt: A Power Automate flow queries a SharePoint list and emails a daily sales summary as an HTML table. Run history shows every run as 'Succeeded' for the past week, but no emails have arrived, and when you inspect a run's HTML table output it's empty. No error was ever raised. How do you troubleshoot this, and what's the likely cause?
questions.modelAnswer:
'Succeeded' in Power Automate's run history only means no action in the flow threw a terminal error - it says nothing about whether each action produced the data it was supposed to. So rather than trusting the status, I'd open an individual recent run and inspect the raw inputs and outputs of each action in sequence, starting with the Get Items (or Get Items filtered) action against the SharePoint list, since that's the most common place a 'succeeded but wrong' failure hides. The most likely cause here is that the OData filter query on that action - probably a date comparison selecting 'today's rows' - stopped matching any rows, which could happen if a column was renamed, a column's data type changed, or the comparison format drifted relative to how SharePoint stores the field. SharePoint's Get Items action doesn't error out when a filter matches zero rows; it just returns an empty array, which then flows cleanly into Create HTML table, which happily renders an empty table, and Send an Email succeeds because sending an empty-but-valid email is not an error condition from the connector's point of view.

Once the empty Get Items output confirms this, I'd fix the filter query to match the current list schema, and more importantly, I'd add a defensive check going forward: a condition action after Get Items that compares the returned item count to zero and sends an explicit alert (to the flow owner, not just silently continuing) if the expected data wasn't found, rather than letting an empty result silently propagate through to a 'successful but useless' email. I'd also review connection health for the flow owner's credentials, since an expiring or re-authenticated connection can sometimes degrade silently in similar ways, and I'd make 'Succeeded' alone an insufficient bar for calling this flow healthy by building that explicit empty-result check into the design.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I always tell people about Power Automate is that 'Succeeded' just means nothing threw a hard error - it doesn't mean the flow did what you wanted. So I wouldn't even look at the overall run status; I'd go straight into one run and open up every action's inputs and outputs, especially Get Items, because that's almost always where this kind of silent failure starts. My bet here is the OData filter on that action - probably filtering for today's date - quietly stopped matching anything, maybe because a column got renamed or its format changed, and SharePoint doesn't treat 'zero rows matched' as an error, it just hands back an empty array that flows straight through to an empty HTML table and a successfully-sent, useless email. Once I confirm that's what happened, I'd fix the filter, but I'd also add a safety net - a simple condition checking if the item count is zero and firing off an alert instead of silently sending nothing - because I never want 'Succeeded' to be the only signal anyone's watching for a business-critical flow like this.
commonMistakes: Treating 'Succeeded' status as proof the flow behaved correctly
Not inspecting individual actions' raw inputs/outputs in run history
Assuming a hard error would always surface if something went wrong
Not checking the filter query against the current list schema for drift (renamed/retyped columns)
Not adding defensive checks (empty-result alerts, Scope/Run After patterns) to catch this class of silent failure
keyPoints: 'Succeeded' status only means no terminal error occurred, not that the output was correct
Inspect each action's raw inputs and outputs in run history to find where data went missing
Zero-row filter matches are a common, non-erroring failure mode in SharePoint connectors
Schema drift (renamed/retyped columns) is a common cause of a filter silently matching nothing
Add explicit empty-result checks and alerts as a defensive design pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the limitation of 'Succeeded' status
Describes correct per-action inspection troubleshooting process
Identifies a plausible root cause (filter/schema mismatch)
Proposes a concrete defensive design fix
Clarity

questions.title: A Scheduled Refresh That Only Times Out on Monday Mornings
questions.prompt: A Power BI semantic model refreshes through an on-premises data gateway against a SQL Server source. The scheduled refresh succeeds every day except Monday mornings, when it reliably fails with a gateway timeout. Manually triggering the refresh an hour later always works. What's your diagnostic process, and what's the likely explanation?
questions.modelAnswer:
A failure pattern that's specific to the first refresh after the weekend points me toward something that happens on weekends and is usually finished by the time someone manually retries an hour later. I'd pull the gateway logs (via the on-premises data gateway app, or the admin center's gateway diagnostics) around the exact failure time to confirm it's genuinely a timeout and not something else masquerading as one, and then I'd ask the DBA or infrastructure team what runs against that SQL Server over the weekend - full backups, index rebuild/reorg maintenance jobs, or a weekly batch catch-up are all common candidates that can still be running early Monday morning and competing hard for I/O and CPU on the source server, or in some cases still holding locks that make the refresh's queries wait. I'd also check whether the gateway machine itself goes through a weekend patch/restart cycle that leaves it under-resourced or still warming up right when the Monday refresh kicks off.

Once I've correlated the failure window against whatever weekend job is actually running, the fix usually has two parts. The immediate mitigation is to shift the Monday refresh time later, past the point where the weekend job reliably finishes, and to add a retry policy with a reasonable delay so a near-miss doesn't require manual intervention. The deeper fix, if this gateway is a single point of failure, is to set up a gateway cluster with two or more members for both resilience and load distribution, and to coordinate directly with whoever owns the weekend maintenance job so its completion time is known and the refresh schedule is deliberately set after it, rather than guessing at a safe gap.
questions.professionalAnswer: A failure that only ever shows up on Monday mornings is basically begging me to look at what happens over the weekend, so that's where I'd go first rather than second-guessing the refresh configuration itself. I'd check the gateway logs right around the failure time to confirm it's a real timeout, and then go ask whoever owns that SQL Server what's running Saturday and Sunday - backups, index maintenance, weekly catch-up jobs - because it's extremely common for one of those to still be running or to have just finished in a way that leaves the server resource-starved right when the scheduled refresh kicks off. The fact that a manual retry an hour later always works is a big clue too - it tells me whatever's contending for resources has usually cleared by then. My fix would be twofold: push the scheduled refresh time later so it's safely past that weekend job's typical finish time, and add a retry policy so a near-miss doesn't need someone to notice and manually rerun it. If the gateway itself turns out to be a single machine with no redundancy, I'd also push to get it clustered, since relying on one box for something this business-critical is its own risk independent of the Monday timing issue.
commonMistakes: Assuming the gateway itself is unreliable without checking logs or correlating with other scheduled jobs
Not investigating what runs on the source server over the weekend before proposing a fix
Simply increasing the timeout without investigating the underlying resource contention
Not considering a single gateway as a point of failure/bottleneck needing a cluster
Not coordinating with the team that owns the weekend maintenance job
keyPoints: Correlate the Monday-only failure pattern with weekend batch/maintenance jobs on the source server
Use gateway logs and admin center diagnostics to confirm the failure is genuinely a timeout
Shifting the refresh schedule later and adding retry policy is the immediate mitigation
A gateway cluster addresses both resilience and resource contention long-term
Cross-team coordination with the source system's maintenance owners is part of the real fix
