questions.title: A #SPILL! Error That Appears Only After the Data Refreshes
questions.prompt: An analyst built a workbook where a dynamic array formula using UNIQUE() and SORT() spills a filtered customer list into adjacent cells, feeding a dashboard elsewhere on the sheet. After the underlying Power Query refreshes with new source data, several downstream formulas start showing #SPILL! errors, even though nobody touched any formulas. Explain why this happens and how you'd prevent it going forward.
questions.modelAnswer:
#SPILL! isn't a formula syntax error - it means Excel knows exactly what the array formula should return, but the range of cells it needs to 'spill' into is blocked by something already occupying one or more of those cells. Dynamic array formulas like UNIQUE() and SORT() don't reserve their spill range in advance; the range is only as large as it needs to be for the current result, which means it can grow or shrink every time the source data changes. After a Power Query refresh brings in more source rows, the UNIQUE() list of customers can simply get longer than it was before, and if the sheet has anything else sitting in the cells just below or beside the original spill range - a hardcoded label, a stray value, or the start of a different formula's own spill range - the growing array now collides with that content and Excel refuses to overwrite it, throwing #SPILL! instead.

The fix is about layout discipline rather than formula logic: keep a deliberate buffer of genuinely empty cells around any dynamic array formula sized for the maximum data volume you realistically expect, not just whatever the list happened to be on the day it was built. Loading the Power Query output into its own dedicated table or sheet, and keeping dynamic array formulas in an isolated area away from manually entered content or other spilling formulas, removes the risk of future growth causing a collision. If the dashboard needs the spilled list referenced elsewhere, I'd reference it via structured references or a named range tied to the spill range (using the # spill operator) rather than hardcoding a fixed range size, so downstream formulas automatically track whatever size the array currently is instead of assuming a fixed row count that will eventually be wrong again.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain to the analyst that #SPILL! doesn't mean the formula broke - it means the formula's answer got bigger than the empty space it has to grow into. UNIQUE() and SORT() don't pre-reserve a block of rows; they just claim exactly as many cells as the current result needs, and if the customer list grew after the refresh pulled in more rows, it's now bumping into whatever's sitting in the cells just below it - probably a label, a hardcoded value, or another formula that used to have room but doesn't anymore. My fix is never to just delete whatever's blocking it and move on, because the exact same thing will happen again next refresh if the list keeps growing. Instead I'd rebuild the layout with real breathing room - put the Power Query output and any dynamic array formulas in their own dedicated area sized for however big that list could realistically get, and if anything downstream needs to reference the spilled range, I'd use the # spill reference so it automatically follows the array's current size instead of pointing at a fixed block of rows that will eventually be too small again.
commonMistakes: Treating #SPILL! as a formula syntax bug rather than a blocked-range issue
Not checking the cells below/beside the formula for content that's now in the way
Placing labels or other content too close to a dynamic array formula's expected growth area
Fixing it once by deleting the blocking content without addressing that it will recur after the next refresh
Hardcoding downstream references to a fixed range size instead of using the # spill reference
keyPoints: #SPILL! means the spill range is blocked, not that the formula is wrong
Dynamic array result size changes whenever the source data volume changes
Keep a genuine empty buffer sized for maximum expected growth around spilling formulas
Isolate Power Query output and dynamic array formulas from manually entered content
Use the # spill reference for downstream formulas instead of a fixed range

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the #SPILL! blocked-range mechanism
Connects the refresh/data-growth trigger to the collision
Proposes concrete layout/prevention fix for the future
Clarity

questions.title: A Mapping Data Flow That Takes Hours on a Dataset That Shouldn't Need It
questions.prompt: A Data Factory mapping data flow joins three source tables (the largest has 8 million rows) and writes to a dimension table. It takes over 3 hours, far longer than the equivalent logic used to take as a SQL stored procedure. The underlying Spark cluster is set to 'General Purpose, 8+8 cores (small).' What would you investigate, and how would you improve this?
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start in the data flow's monitoring/debug view and look at the per-transformation timings rather than guessing, because '3 hours for 8 million rows' almost always has one dominant bottleneck stage rather than being uniformly slow everywhere. Common culprits at this scale: a join that isn't using partitioned, pushed-down reads from the source (meaning Spark pulls far more data across the wire than it needs to before filtering), a broadcast join setting misapplied to a table that isn't actually small enough to broadcast efficiently, a sink configured to write through a single partition instead of writing in parallel, or an unnecessary Sort or exists/lookup transformation that forces materializing the full dataset before it needs to. I'd also check the cluster configuration itself - whether it's using an existing warm pool or cold-starting on every run, since startup/TTL overhead can eat meaningful time on a job this size, and whether 'small General Purpose' is simply undersized for a three-way join at this row count versus a Memory Optimized tier built for join-heavy work.

Once I've found the dominant stage, I'd fix it directly: enable source partitioning on the join keys, correct the broadcast join setting so only genuinely small reference tables are broadcast, tune the sink's partitioning/batch size for parallel writes, and scale the cluster size or type if the per-transformation timings show raw compute capacity is actually the constraint rather than a design issue. But I'd also step back and ask whether a mapping data flow is even the right tool here: if both source and destination are the same relational SQL Server engine and the transformation is a straightforward three-table join feeding a dimension, a native T-SQL stored procedure or an ADF Copy activity plus a stored-procedure activity doing a set-based MERGE would very likely outperform spinning up a Spark cluster for this, which is probably exactly why the old stored procedure was faster - sometimes the fix isn't tuning the data flow, it's recognizing the workload doesn't need Spark at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I touch any settings, I'd open up the data flow's monitoring view and look at where the time is actually going stage by stage, because at three hours for 8 million rows, there's almost certainly one transformation eating most of that time rather than everything being equally slow. I'd specifically check whether the source reads are getting pushed down and partitioned or whether Spark is pulling way more data than it needs before filtering, and I'd check the join settings for a broadcast join applied to something that isn't actually small - that's a classic way to tank performance. I'd also just ask the obvious question: is the cluster cold-starting every run, and is 'small General Purpose' really sized for a three-way join at this volume. But honestly, the bigger thing I'd flag to the team is that if the source and the destination are both the same SQL Server, and the old stored procedure did this fine, maybe the real fix isn't tuning the data flow at all - maybe a data flow was the wrong tool for a relational-to-relational job like this in the first place, and a Copy activity plus a set-based MERGE in a stored procedure would just be faster and cheaper than any amount of Spark tuning.
commonMistakes: Jumping to 'scale up the cluster' without first checking per-transformation timings to find the actual bottleneck
Not checking whether source reads are partitioned/pushed down versus pulling full tables
Misapplying a broadcast join to a table that isn't actually small
Not considering that a mapping data flow (Spark) may be the wrong tool when source and sink are the same relational engine
Ignoring sink write partitioning/batching as a contributor to total runtime
keyPoints: Use the data flow monitoring view to isolate the actual bottleneck stage before changing anything
Check source partitioning/pushdown and broadcast join correctness
Tune sink write partitioning/batch size for parallel writes
Evaluate cluster sizing and cold-start/TTL overhead
Reconsider whether a mapping data flow is the right tool versus native T-SQL for relational-to-relational transforms

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses monitoring to isolate the bottleneck rather than guessing
Identifies partitioning/broadcast join issues correctly
Proposes concrete cluster/sink tuning fixes
Questions the tool choice (data flow vs native T-SQL) appropriately
Clarity

questions.title: When an Indexed View Is Worth the Write Cost
questions.prompt: Your reporting dashboard runs an aggregation query against Production.Product (grouped by subcategory, computing a row count and total list price) hundreds of times per minute during business hours, and the underlying table is only touched by a handful of transactions a day. A teammate suggests materializing this aggregation as an indexed view. Walk through the real requirements for making that work, what SQL Server does differently once it's in place, and the ongoing cost you're trading for speed. Would you recommend it here -- and would your answer change if the table instead took thousands of writes per second?
questions.modelAnswer:
A regular view is just stored SQL text -- it re-runs its underlying SELECT every time it's queried. An indexed view is the one case where that's not true: once you create a unique clustered index on the view, SQL Server physically materializes the computed result set on disk, and queries against the view (or, on Enterprise edition, queries against the base table that the optimizer recognizes as equivalent) can read that pre-computed data directly instead of re-aggregating Production.Product every time.

Getting there has real, non-negotiable requirements: the view must be created WITH SCHEMABINDING, which locks the underlying table's structure so SQL Server can guarantee the view stays consistent with it -- you can't ALTER a schemabound table's referenced columns without dropping dependent objects first. Aggregations must use COUNT_BIG(*), not COUNT(*). A number of T-SQL constructs are disallowed inside the view's definition (TOP, several non-deterministic or imprecise functions, certain outer join shapes). And on non-Enterprise editions, the optimizer won't automatically substitute the indexed view for an equivalent base-table query -- you need the NOEXPAND hint to force it.

The cost is real and ongoing: every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against Production.Product now has to maintain the materialized aggregate too, on top of the base table write. For this scenario -- read-heavy by a wide margin, with only a dozen or so writes a day -- that tradeoff is clearly worth it: you're paying a trivial amount of extra write overhead a handful of times daily to make hundreds of reads per minute avoid re-aggregating the table from scratch. If the table instead took thousands of writes per second, I'd recommend against it: the indexed view's maintenance cost would be paid on every single one of those writes, compounding exactly where you can least afford it, and I'd look at a separate pre-aggregated reporting table refreshed on a schedule, or a different caching layer, instead.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame it for the team: a normal view is free to create because it doesn't store anything -- it's just a saved query. An indexed view is different, and the trigger for that difference is adding a unique clustered index to it; the moment you do, SQL Server actually materializes the result on disk. To even get there you need WITH SCHEMABINDING on the view, COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT, and you have to accept that the view's definition is now more restricted -- no TOP, limited function support. And if we're not on Enterprise, I'd flag that the optimizer won't use it automatically; we'd need NOEXPAND in the query, or it just does the full aggregation anyway and we got nothing for the extra complexity.

The real decision point for me is the read/write ratio. In this case we've got maybe a dozen writes a day against hundreds of reads a minute, so I'd absolutely recommend the indexed view -- we're trading a tiny bit of extra work on writes that barely happen for a big win on reads that happen constantly. But if someone told me this table was taking thousands of writes a second, I'd push back hard on the same idea, because now every one of those writes has to keep the materialized aggregate in sync, and that's exactly the kind of hidden cost that tanks throughput on a hot table. In that case I'd rather build a separate summary table refreshed on a schedule, or push the aggregation into a different layer entirely.
questions.example:
CREATE VIEW dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary
WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID,
       COUNT_BIG(*) AS ProductCount,
       SUM(ListPrice) AS TotalListPrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE ProductSubcategoryID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;
GO

CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_vw_ProductPriceSummary
ON dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary (ProductSubcategoryID);
GO

-- On Standard edition, force the optimizer to use the materialized data:
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, ProductCount, TotalListPrice
FROM dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary WITH (NOEXPAND);
commonMistakes: Forgetting WITH SCHEMABINDING, which indexed views require
Using COUNT(*) instead of the required COUNT_BIG(*)
Assuming the optimizer auto-uses the indexed view outside Enterprise edition without NOEXPAND
Ignoring write amplification and recommending indexed views for high-write tables
Not accounting for how SCHEMABINDING restricts future ALTER TABLE changes to the base table
keyPoints: Unique clustered index is what actually materializes the view's data
WITH SCHEMABINDING and COUNT_BIG(*) are mandatory requirements
Non-Enterprise editions need the NOEXPAND hint to use the indexed view
Every write to the base table now also maintains the materialized aggregate
Worth it for read-heavy, low-write-ratio reporting aggregations
Not worth it for tables with very high write throughput
