Names the real requirements (SCHEMABINDING, COUNT_BIG, restrictions)
Explains the ongoing write-maintenance cost
Gives a correct, justified recommendation for the low-write scenario
Correctly reverses the recommendation for the high-write scenario with reasoning
Mentions NOEXPAND / edition behavior

questions.title: Designing Dynamic RLS for 40 Sales Territories
questions.prompt: A company has 40 sales territories, each with its own manager who should only see their own territory's data, and the territory list changes periodically as the business reorganizes. Design the row-level security approach - don't just name the feature, walk through the actual model changes, the role definition, and how you'd validate it before any real manager is assigned.
questions.modelAnswer: Forty territories rules out a static role per value immediately - that's 40 roles to create and maintain by hand every time the org chart changes, and someone has to remember to add a 41st when the business adds a territory. The right design is a single dynamic role whose filter expression adapts to whoever is signed in, backed by a small user-mapping table added to the model: two columns, UserEmail and TerritoryID, with one row per manager, related to the territory dimension. The role's DAX filter expression is simply [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME() on that mapping table - one role, one expression, scaling to any number of territories because the filtering logic never changes, only the rows in the mapping table do. A critical detail: USERNAME() and USERPRINCIPALNAME() return different formats depending on where the report runs - USERNAME() returns DOMAIN\username in Desktop but a UPN in the service, while USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns a UPN-style value, like an email, in both places. Whichever function the role uses, the mapping table's values have to match the format that function actually returns when the report is viewed in the Power BI service, which is where real managers will view it, not necessarily what it shows while testing in Desktop. Before assigning a single real person, I'd validate with Test as role: select the role, confirm the report filters down to exactly one territory's data, and check that it matches the identity shown under 'Now viewing as.' The real limitation to flag: Test as role evaluates the filter using my own identity, so USERPRINCIPALNAME() inside the test returns my UPN, not the UPN of the manager I'm trying to simulate - it genuinely proves the filter logic works, but it can't prove a specific external manager will see the right data once onboarded. For that, the manager has to actually sign in and view it themselves, which I'd do for at least one real manager as a final check before rolling the role out to all 40.
questions.professionalAnswer: With 40 territories, I wouldn't even consider a static role per value - that's 40 things to build and maintain, and it falls apart the moment the org reorganizes. I'd build one dynamic role instead, backed by a small user-mapping table I add to the model: a UserEmail column and a TerritoryID column, related to the territory dimension, with one row per manager. The role's filter is just [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(), and because that's the only logic, adding or removing a territory becomes a data update to the mapping table, not a model or role change. The detail I'd be careful about is that USERNAME() and USERPRINCIPALNAME() don't necessarily return the same format in Desktop as they do once published to the service, so whichever function I pick, I need the mapping table's values to match what that function actually returns in the service, since that's where managers will really view it. Before putting a single real person on this, I'd use Test as role to confirm the filter narrows down to one territory correctly - but I'd be upfront that Test as role is checking the logic using my own identity, not proving what an actual colleague will see, so I'd still have at least one real manager sign in and verify their own view before rolling this out to all 40.
questions.example: Mapping table: UserMapping(UserEmail, TerritoryID) with 40 rows, one per manager, related to DimTerritory[TerritoryID]. Role 'Territory Manager' filter: [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(). Reorg handling: adding/removing a territory is an UPDATE to UserMapping, not a change to the role or the model.
commonMistakes: Building 40 static roles instead of one dynamic role with a mapping table
Assuming USERNAME() and USERPRINCIPALNAME() return the same format in Desktop and the service
Treating a successful Test as role result as proof a specific external manager will see correct data
Forgetting the mapping table needs a real relationship to the territory data for the filter to actually propagate
keyPoints: A single dynamic role with a user-mapping table scales to any number of territories
USERPRINCIPALNAME()/USERNAME() format must match what's stored in the mapping table as seen in the service
Test as role validates filter logic using your own identity, not the target user's
Reorganizations become data updates to the mapping table, not model/role changes
Final validation should include a real manager signing in, not just Test as role

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes a single dynamic role + user-mapping table design
Explains the USERNAME/USERPRINCIPALNAME format gotcha
Describes Test as role validation steps
Correctly states the limitation of Test as role and the real-user validation step
Addresses maintainability as territories change

questions.title: Choosing Between Star and Snowflake for a New Retail Warehouse
questions.prompt: You're designing the dimensional model for a new retail analytics warehouse feeding both Power BI and Tableau. The Product dimension has a genuine hierarchy (Product -> Subcategory -> Category -> Department) with attributes that change at different rates. A junior analyst argues for fully normalizing this into a snowflake schema to 'save space and avoid redundancy.' How do you decide, and what do you tell the team?
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd push back gently on the 'save space' framing first, because it's the part most likely to be wrong here. In a columnar, compressed engine - which is what both Power BI's VertiPaq and most modern cloud warehouses are - repeated hierarchy values like Category and Department compress extremely well inside a single denormalized Product dimension; the storage savings a snowflake would theoretically provide are largely illusory once you account for how little a dictionary-encoded repeated string actually costs. What a snowflake does unambiguously cost is query simplicity: every additional join the analyst (or Tableau's live-connection engine, or DirectQuery) has to traverse to get from a fact row to the Department label adds complexity to both ad hoc self-service exploration and to performance, since joins across multiple dimension tables are strictly more expensive than reading columns off one flat dimension.

My default for a BI-facing warehouse feeding self-service tools is star schema, with snowflaking reserved for cases where it actually earns its keep - typically a genuinely large reference dimension that's maintained independently on its own ETL cadence and shared across many fact tables, where keeping it as its own table avoids real duplication-of-maintenance-effort, not just duplication-of-bytes. The Product hierarchy described here doesn't meet that bar; it's a single dimension's own attribute hierarchy, not a shared independently-changing reference table, so I'd keep it flat. I'd frame this to the team around three criteria going forward: how it affects self-service analyst experience, how it affects Power BI/Tableau query performance given their specific join-handling characteristics, and whether compression already solves the 'redundancy' concern - which, for VertiPaq, it almost always does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team straight up that 'save space' isn't really the strong argument it sounds like, especially once this lands in Power BI - VertiPaq compresses repeated category and department values so well that snowflaking barely moves the storage needle, but it absolutely moves the complexity needle for anyone trying to write a quick DAX measure or build a Tableau view against it. My default is always star schema for anything feeding self-service BI, because every extra join between the fact table and the final attribute is friction - for analysts writing queries and for the engine executing them. I'd only reach for snowflaking a sub-dimension if it's genuinely large and maintained on its own independent schedule across multiple fact tables, where keeping it separate actually saves real engineering effort, not just bytes. This Product hierarchy doesn't look like that case to me - it's one dimension's own natural hierarchy, so I'd keep it flat and explain to the junior analyst why 'normalized' isn't automatically 'better' once you're optimizing for a BI engine instead of an OLTP system.
commonMistakes: Optimizing for storage savings in a columnar/compressed engine where the savings barely matter
Not considering the self-service analyst experience cost of extra joins
Snowflaking a dimension that isn't actually large or independently maintained
Ignoring tool-specific implications like DirectQuery join depth or Tableau join/relationship complexity
Treating this as an academic 3NF question rather than a BI performance/usability tradeoff
keyPoints: Star schema is the default for BI-facing, self-service-oriented models
Columnar compression (VertiPaq) largely eliminates the storage-saving argument for snowflaking
Snowflaking is justified only for large, independently-maintained shared reference dimensions
Consider tool-specific implications for Power BI and Tableau
Frame the decision around analyst usability, not academic normalization theory

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Argues for star schema default with sound, specific reasoning
Correctly addresses the storage/compression misconception
Defines a clear bar for when snowflaking is actually justified
Considers tool-specific implications (Power BI/Tableau)
Communicates persuasively to the team

questions.title: Import, DirectQuery, or Composite for a Near-Real-Time Operations Dashboard
questions.prompt: Operations wants a Power BI dashboard showing warehouse throughput 'as close to real-time as possible,' built on a 2-billion-row fact table in a SQL Server warehouse alongside several small, slow-changing dimension tables. Walk through how you'd decide between Import, DirectQuery, and a composite model, and justify your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Pure Import is ruled out quickly at 2 billion rows: even with VertiPaq's compression, importing and then refreshing a table of that size frequently enough to feel 'near real-time' isn't realistic, and a full import of that scale is itself a heavy operation. Pure DirectQuery is tempting given the real-time requirement, but it comes with real costs at this scale: every slicer and filter interaction fires a live query against a 2-billion-row table, DAX functionality is restricted (no complex iterators or certain time-intelligence patterns), and interactive performance degrades noticeably compared to Import, which usually makes a 'DirectQuery because real-time' decision backfire on user experience exactly when people are watching it most closely.

My recommendation is a composite model: import the small, slow-changing dimension tables outright, since there's no cost to having them fully resident and fast, and handle the fact table with a layered approach rather than a single storage mode - build a Power BI aggregation table at a coarser grain (say, hourly throughput summaries) in Import mode for the default views most users interact with, and let DirectQuery handle drill-through to the full-grain detail only when someone actually drills into specifics. This gives fast, fully-functional default dashboards most of the time while still exposing near-real-time detail on demand, which is usually what 'as close to real-time as possible' actually means once you ask stakeholders what they're trying to do rather than taking the phrase literally. I'd also flag Direct Lake (if the organization is on Fabric capacity) as a newer alternative worth evaluating, since it avoids some of the Import/DirectQuery tradeoff entirely by querying Parquet files directly without a traditional import cycle - but either way, before committing to an architecture I'd pin down the actual acceptable staleness window with Operations, because 'real-time' and 'refreshed every 15 minutes' often turn out to satisfy the same underlying need.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move isn't actually to pick a storage mode - it's to go back to Operations and ask what 'near-real-time' really means to them in practice, because very often a 15-minute scheduled refresh satisfies the actual need and saves everyone a lot of architectural pain. But assuming they genuinely need live or near-live numbers against 2 billion rows, pure Import is off the table because you can't refresh that volume frequently enough, and pure DirectQuery worries me because every interaction becomes a live query against a huge table with restricted DAX - that's a rough experience exactly when people are watching the dashboard closely. So I'd go composite: import the small dimensions since there's no downside, and for the fact table I'd build an imported aggregation at a coarser grain for the default view, with DirectQuery wired up for drill-through when someone actually needs full-grain detail. That combination gets most users a fast, fully capable dashboard while still giving anyone who drills in real freshness. If the org's on Fabric, I'd also put Direct Lake on the table as a genuinely different way to sidestep this whole tradeoff, but either way I'm not committing to an architecture until I know the real freshness requirement and I've checked that the SQL Server source is indexed well enough to support whatever DirectQuery traffic does end up hitting it.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to DirectQuery purely because the word 'real-time' was used, without weighing the performance/DAX cost at this scale
Defaulting to Import without checking whether refresh frequency can meet the actual freshness requirement
Not knowing about Power BI aggregation tables and the drill-through composite pattern
Not addressing the need to tune SQL Server indexing to support DirectQuery's generated queries
Not clarifying the actual acceptable staleness window with stakeholders before committing to an architecture
keyPoints: Composite model with an imported aggregation plus DirectQuery drill-through is the practical middle ground
DirectQuery has real performance and DAX-functionality costs at billion-row scale
Import alone can't meet near-real-time freshness requirements at this volume
Clarify the actual business freshness requirement before committing to an architecture
Mention Direct Lake/Fabric as a modern alternative worth evaluating

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly weighs Import vs DirectQuery tradeoffs at this scale
Recommends and justifies a composite/aggregation-with-drill-through design
Addresses source-side indexing/performance needs for DirectQuery
Clarifies the actual business freshness requirement before architecting
Mentions modern alternatives (Direct Lake) where relevant

questions.title: Designing RLS for Managers With Overlapping, Combined Roles
questions.prompt: You need to design row-level security for a sales model where regional managers see only their own region, a few global executives should see everything, some category managers need their category across every region, and a handful of people hold combined roles - for example, a regional manager who is also a category manager somewhere else. How do you architect the RLS model, and what specific risks do you design around?
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd avoid creating a static role per combination of region and category - that approach doesn't scale and gets unmanageable the moment a second combined-access person shows up. Instead I'd build a small, data-driven entitlement table (UserEmail, AccessType, AccessValue) that lives outside the model, ideally synced from an HR or identity source, and define only a handful of roles in the model itself - Regional, Category, and Global - each with a DAX filter expression that checks this entitlement table via USERPRINCIPALNAME() rather than hardcoding a role per manager. Adding or removing someone's access then becomes a data change in the entitlement table, not a model redeploy.

The specific risk I design around hardest is that Power BI unions permissions across every role a user belongs to rather than intersecting them - so a regional manager who is also a category manager elsewhere needs to be deliberately tested to confirm they see exactly the union of their region plus their category, and nothing broader. I'd also explicitly design around the workspace-role bypass: RLS only applies to Viewer-level or app access, so any of these managers who also happen to have Contributor or Admin rights on the workspace would see everything regardless of role assignment, which has to be prevented by workspace access policy, not by anything in the DAX. For global executives, I'd use an explicit AllAccess flag in the entitlement table rather than a hardcoded unrestricted role, since that's easier to audit later. Finally, I'd treat this as an ongoing governance process rather than a one-time build - a periodic access review of the entitlement table, and mandatory testing of every combined-role scenario as part of UAT before go-live, since RLS is a security control and deserves the same rigor as one.
questions.professionalAnswer: My instinct is to not build a role for every possible combination of region and category, because that's a maintenance nightmare the second someone's access changes. I'd build a small entitlement table outside the model - who gets what region, category, or global access - and have just a few DAX roles that look that table up dynamically, so changing someone's access is a data edit, not a model change. The thing I'd specifically test hardest, because it bites people constantly, is that Power BI doesn't intersect multiple roles - it unions them. So that regional-manager-who's-also-a-category-manager-elsewhere has to be verified to see exactly region-plus-category and nothing more, not some unexpected broader combination. I'd also make sure none of these managers have Contributor or Admin rights on the workspace, because RLS just doesn't apply to those roles regardless of how carefully I've built the DAX - that's a workspace-permissions conversation, not a modeling one. And for the global executives, I'd rather give them an explicit flag in the entitlement table than a separate 'sees everything' role, just because it's easier to audit later who actually has that kind of access and why.
commonMistakes: Creating a static role per combination of region/category instead of a scalable data-driven entitlement table
Not understanding that multiple role membership unions access rather than intersecting it
Forgetting that workspace Contributor/Admin/Member roles bypass RLS regardless of role assignment
Treating RLS as a one-time setup rather than an ongoing governed access-review process
Not explicitly testing combined-role users before go-live
keyPoints: Data-driven entitlement table scales far better than static per-combination roles
Dynamic RLS via USERPRINCIPALNAME looked up against the entitlement table
Multiple role membership unions permissions - must be explicitly tested for combined-role users
Workspace-role RLS bypass risk must be addressed via access policy, not DAX
Treat RLS as an ongoing governance process with periodic access review

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a scalable data-driven entitlement design
Correctly addresses the multi-role union risk with testing
Addresses the workspace-role bypass risk
Discusses ongoing governance/review process
Clarity

questions.title: Designing Error Handling for a Multi-Stage ADF Pipeline
questions.prompt: You're designing a Data Factory pipeline with five sequential stages: extract from an external API, land to ADLS, validate schema, transform via a mapping data flow, and load to the warehouse. Some failures should retry automatically, some should alert and stop, and a partial failure midway through shouldn't leave the warehouse in an inconsistent state. Describe your error-handling and retry architecture.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd tailor retry behavior to the type of failure rather than applying one blanket policy. The API extract stage gets an activity-level retry count and interval tuned for transient network issues and rate-limit throttling, ideally respecting any rate-limit headers the API returns. The schema validation stage, by contrast, should never auto-retry, because retrying bad data doesn't fix it - instead I'd route a validation failure through an explicit 'Run After: Failed' branch into a Scope activity dedicated to error handling, which logs the specific failure details to a monitoring table or Log Analytics and triggers an alert (via a webhook, Logic App, or Teams connector) before stopping the pipeline, rather than relying on ADF's default stop-on-failure behavior alone.

For the consistency concern, the load stage is the part I'd design most carefully: rather than loading directly into the final warehouse tables, I'd land transformed data into a staging table first and only promote it into the final tables via an atomic MERGE or table-swap once the staging load has fully succeeded and passed any final checks - a 'stage then promote' pattern that guarantees a failure between landing and promotion never leaves the warehouse partially updated. I'd also use watermarks or pipeline parameters so that a rerun after any failure resumes safely without duplicating data that already landed successfully. All of this gets centralized into Log Analytics or a custom logging table keyed by pipeline run ID, stage, status, and error message, feeding the Monitor hub and alerting, with a clear runbook defining who owns each category of alert - an API failure versus a data-quality failure are different people's problems, and that should be explicit rather than assumed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't put the same retry policy on every activity in this pipeline - that's the first mistake I'd avoid. The API extract gets real retries with backoff, since that's a classic transient-failure situation, but schema validation failing should never retry automatically, because retrying the same bad data just wastes time and can hide a real data-quality issue from the people who need to see it. For that, I'd build an explicit failure branch using Run After and a Scope activity that logs what went wrong and fires an alert, rather than just letting the pipeline die quietly in the Monitor hub where nobody's watching. The part I'd spend the most design time on is the load stage, because that's where 'partial failure leaves things inconsistent' actually bites you - so I'd never load straight into the final warehouse tables. I'd land into staging first and only promote into the real tables with an atomic swap or MERGE once staging is fully validated, so there's no window where the warehouse is sitting half-updated. And I'd make sure reruns are safe by using watermarks, so if something does fail, resuming doesn't double-load anything that already succeeded.
commonMistakes: Applying blanket retry policies to every activity regardless of whether the failure type is actually transient
Relying only on ADF's default stop-on-failure behavior without explicit Run After branches for logging and alerting
Loading directly into final warehouse tables, risking partial/inconsistent writes on mid-pipeline failure
Not using watermarks or parameters to make reruns safe and idempotent
Not centralizing error logging/alerting, leaving failures invisible outside the Monitor hub UI
keyPoints: Tailor retry policy to failure type - transient errors retry, non-retryable errors (like schema validation) do not
Explicit Run After failure branches with Scope activities for structured logging and alerting
Stage-then-promote load pattern guarantees warehouse consistency on partial failure
Watermark-based design makes reruns safe without duplicating already-landed data
Centralized logging with clear ownership per alert category

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Differentiates retry strategy by failure type
Designs an explicit failure-branch/alerting pattern
Addresses consistency via staging/idempotent load design
Addresses safe reruns via watermarking
Clarity

questions.title: Designing a Code-Review Workflow for Power BI Report Changes
questions.prompt: Six analysts all edit the same set of Power BI reports and the shared semantic model directly in the Service, and changes occasionally break visuals or measures for everyone with no review step. Leadership wants a Git-based review process. Describe the workflow, and be honest about the real constraints you have to design around given that Power BI content isn't naturally diffable text.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first and most important move is getting off the traditional .pbix binary format for anything that's going to live under Git review, and onto the Power BI Project (.pbip) format, which serializes the report layout and the semantic model as readable JSON/TMDL folders instead of an opaque binary - without that change, 'Git-based review' is really just file storage, since a binary diff tells a reviewer nothing. With .pbip in place, the workflow looks like normal software development: analysts work on feature branches in Desktop, commit their .pbip changes, and open a pull request; reviewers read the TMDL/JSON diff to understand exactly what measures or model relationships changed, and also open the branch in Desktop to visually check the report before approving, since even a text-diffable model format doesn't make a changed chart layout meaningfully reviewable as text. Branch protection requires at least one approval before merge, and promotion from Dev to Test to Production workspaces happens through a deployment pipeline (Power BI Deployment Pipelines, or a scripted deploy via the Fabric/Power BI REST API in a CI job) triggered only from the main branch - never a direct publish from someone's Desktop straight into Production.

I'd be upfront with leadership about the real limits here: visual/layout changes are still genuinely hard to review as a diff even in TMDL format, so reviewers need to actually open and look at the report, not just read JSON; and the same report being edited on two branches at once is still a painful, mostly-manual merge conflict to resolve, since this isn't line-based collaborative text editing the way code is. This also requires a real culture shift for analysts used to live-editing in the Service - I'd recommend keeping a separate 'self-service sandbox' workspace where ad hoc, ungoverned edits are still fine, and reserving the Git-reviewed workflow specifically for the curated, widely-consumed production reports and the shared semantic model, rather than trying to force every edit through PR review.
questions.professionalAnswer: Step one, honestly, is getting everyone off .pbix and onto the .pbip project format, because a binary file in Git is basically just backup storage - nobody can meaningfully review a diff of it. Once we're on .pbip, this starts to look like a normal PR workflow: branch, commit, open a pull request, and a reviewer can actually read the TMDL diff to see what measure or relationship changed, plus open it in Desktop to eyeball the visual layout before approving. I'd set up branch protection requiring at least one approval, and route Dev-to-Test-to-Prod promotion through a deployment pipeline triggered from main, not someone manually publishing from their own machine. But I'd tell leadership straight up that this isn't going to be as clean as reviewing code - layout and visual changes still need an actual human look, not just a JSON diff, and if two people touch the same report on different branches at the same time, that merge conflict is still going to be painful to resolve. And this is as much a habit change as a tooling change, so I'd keep a separate sandbox workspace where people can still just edit live for quick personal stuff, and reserve this whole governed process for the reports that actually matter broadly.
commonMistakes: Assuming .pbix files can be meaningfully reviewed in Git without adopting .pbip/TMDL format
Underestimating that visual/layout changes still require manual visual review even with text-diffable model changes
Not separating curated, governed production reports from ad hoc self-service sandboxes
Manually publishing from Desktop to Production instead of using deployment pipelines for promotion
Ignoring the retraining/culture change needed for analysts used to live-editing in the Service
keyPoints: Adopt .pbip/TMDL project format as the prerequisite for meaningful Git diffs
PR-based review workflow with branch protection and a required approval
Deployment pipelines for Dev/Test/Prod promotion, never direct Desktop-to-Prod publishing
Honestly acknowledge visual-diff and merge-conflict limitations requiring manual review
Distinguish governed production reports from self-service sandbox workspaces

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes .pbip/TMDL as the enabler for diffable review
Designs a realistic PR plus deployment-pipeline workflow
Honestly addresses visual-diff and merge-conflict limitations
Addresses governance/culture considerations

questions.title: A CI/CD Strategy Spanning dbt, T-SQL, and Power BI
questions.prompt: Your analytics stack has dbt models, hand-written T-SQL stored procedures, and Power BI semantic models, all needing to move safely from dev to test to production. Design an end-to-end CI/CD strategy covering all three, including what runs automatically on every pull request versus what requires manual promotion.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd put all three codebases under Git with environment-specific configuration externalized rather than hardcoded - dbt profiles/targets per environment, SQL Server connection strings pulled from Key Vault, and Power BI deployment pipeline stages - so the same code behaves correctly wherever it's promoted to. On every pull request, CI runs a consistent set of automatic, required-to-pass gates: dbt build and test against an ephemeral or shared dev schema to validate models and data tests, T-SQL changes get run through lightweight tests (tSQLt unit tests, or a script executing procs against a test database and asserting expected results) plus SQL linting, and for Power BI, if the team has adopted .pbip/TMDL, a model validation step using something like Tabular Editor's command-line best-practice-analyzer rules or a basic schema diff. None of this touches Test or Production directly; it only validates the PR before merge.

Manual promotion is reserved specifically for Test and Production deployment. Merging to main can trigger automatic deployment to Test, but Production promotion requires an explicit human approval gate - GitHub Environments with required reviewers, or someone manually triggering the Power BI Deployment Pipeline's production stage - because a bad semantic model refresh or schema change can break dashboards people are actively using, and that deserves a deliberate, business-hours-aware human decision rather than full automation. I'd also insist on versioned migration scripts for T-SQL changes rather than ad hoc proc edits directly in Production, so database schema changes get the same promotion discipline as everything else, and I'd keep all secrets in Key Vault or GitHub Secrets with least-privilege, environment-scoped credentials rather than anywhere in the repository itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat all three - dbt, T-SQL, and Power BI - as needing the same basic promotion discipline, even though the specific checks look different for each. On every PR, I want automatic, required checks: dbt build and test against a dev schema, some kind of T-SQL test (even lightweight tSQLt tests or a script that runs the procs and checks results) plus a linter, and if we're on .pbip for Power BI, a model validation pass. None of that touches anything beyond dev, it's just the gate before merge. Where I'd deliberately slow things down is Production - merging to main can auto-deploy to Test, but Production needs an actual human to approve the promotion, especially for the Power BI semantic model, because breaking a live dashboard refresh is a very different kind of incident than a failed dev build. I'd also make sure T-SQL changes go through versioned migration scripts instead of someone editing a proc directly in Prod, so the database gets the same rigor as the code, and obviously none of the connection strings or API keys live anywhere but Key Vault or GitHub Secrets, scoped tightly per environment.
commonMistakes: Treating Power BI as impossible to include in CI/CD and leaving it as a disconnected manual-only process
Automatically deploying production-impacting changes without a human approval gate
Not testing T-SQL changes at all because there's no dbt-equivalent test framework assumed
Storing credentials/connection strings in repo configuration instead of a secrets manager
Not distinguishing automatic PR-gate checks from deliberate, approved Production promotion
keyPoints: Unify dbt, T-SQL, and Power BI under one Git-based promotion model with externalized environment config
Automatic PR gates: dbt tests, T-SQL tests/lint, Power BI model validation
Manual, human-approved gate specifically before Production promotion
Versioned T-SQL migrations instead of ad hoc Production edits
Centralized secrets management with least-privilege, environment-scoped credentials

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a coherent end-to-end pipeline covering all three technologies
Correctly separates automatic PR checks from manual Production promotion
Addresses T-SQL testing/migration strategy specifically
Addresses secrets/security management
Clarity

questions.title: Extracts or Live Connection for a Finance Close Dashboard
questions.prompt: Finance wants a Tableau dashboard against the general ledger that must reflect accurate numbers during month-end close, when figures change multiple times per hour, but outside of close week the same dashboard serves slower historical trend analysis for 50+ casual viewers. How do you architect the connection strategy, and would you use the same approach in both situations?
questions.modelAnswer:
I wouldn't use one connection strategy for both situations, because the two scenarios have genuinely different priorities and usage patterns. During close week, correctness and freshness matter more than interactive snappiness, and the actual usage is a small, focused finance team working hard against live numbers, so a live connection (or an extract refreshing very frequently, every 15-30 minutes, if a direct live connection proves too slow for interactive use) is justified there despite the performance cost, because serving someone a stale number during close is a worse outcome than a slightly slower click. Outside close week, the same correctness urgency doesn't apply - the 50+ casual viewers doing trend analysis don't need numbers that are fresher than daily, and a standard extract, refreshed on a normal schedule, gives them a dramatically more responsive dashboard while taking real load off the GL system.

My recommendation is two distinct artifacts rather than forcing one workbook to serve both needs: a live-connected (or high-frequency-refresh) version clearly labeled and restricted to the close-week finance team, and a daily-extract version for the broader 50-person audience, each with a visible 'last refreshed' or 'as of' indicator so nobody is confused about which freshness guarantee they're looking at. I'd also make sure the GL source is protected during close week - appropriate indexing or a dedicated reporting view, and awareness of how many concurrent live queries the close team's usage generates - since a live connection serving even a small team hard during a high-activity week still needs the source system to hold up. Governance-wise, access to the close-week live version should be restricted to finance, while the historical extract version can have broader read access, since the risk profile and audience are different.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't force one approach to cover both of these, because they're really asking for different things. Close week is about correctness over speed - a small finance team actively working, needing the latest numbers even if that means living with live-connection performance, or at worst an extract refreshing every 15-30 minutes if live proves too clunky to use interactively. The rest of the month is the opposite problem: 50-plus casual viewers who don't need anything fresher than daily, and who'd be much better served by a fast, standard extract that also takes pressure off the GL system. So my actual recommendation is two separate artifacts - a live or near-live version scoped to finance during close, and a daily-extract version for general trend viewing - each clearly labeled with a last-refreshed indicator so nobody's confused about which one they're looking at. I'd also make sure the GL system itself is protected during close week, since even a small team hitting it live repeatedly during a high-activity period needs decent indexing or a dedicated reporting view to hold up, and I'd restrict access to the close-week version to finance specifically rather than opening it broadly like the historical version.
commonMistakes: Picking one connection type for all use cases without weighing concurrency, freshness need, and audience separately
Using a live connection for the 50-casual-viewer case and unnecessarily overloading the GL system
Using an extract-only approach for the close-week case and giving finance stale numbers during a critical period
Not adding a visible 'last refreshed'/as-of indicator so users know which freshness mode they're seeing
Ignoring source-system load/protection considerations during the live-connection period
keyPoints: Usage pattern (concurrency, freshness need, audience) should drive connection choice, not a single blanket rule
Separate live and extract-based artifacts for genuinely different needs rather than one workbook forced to serve both
Protect the source GL system from live-query load during high-activity close weeks
Visible freshness indicators prevent confusion about which version a user is viewing
Different governance/access scope for close-week versus general-use versions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Argues against a one-size-fits-all connection strategy with clear reasoning
Proposes a workable dual-artifact design
Addresses source-system protection during live use
Addresses governance/freshness transparency
Clarity

questions.title: Designing a Semantic Model Analysts Can Self-Serve From Safely
questions.prompt: Leadership wants 30+ business analysts across departments to build their own Power BI reports against a shared semantic model instead of requesting custom reports from your BI team, but is worried about 'everyone creating their own version of revenue.' How do you design the semantic layer and governance around it to make self-service actually work?
questions.modelAnswer:
The design principle I'd start from is that analysts shouldn't be building their own revenue logic at all - they should be building reports on top of a single, centrally-owned semantic model that already encapsulates core business logic as reusable, well-named, documented measures like Total Revenue, Net Revenue, and YoY Growth. Rather than exposing raw fact and dimension tables and trusting 30 different people to compute consistent definitions, I'd hide raw/implementation columns from report view and expose only the fields and measures intended for direct use, so there's effectively one correct way to get 'Revenue' and it's already built for them. I'd apply the Service's Certified and Promoted endorsement labels to this model specifically so analysts can tell at a glance which dataset is the trusted source of truth versus any personal or experimental dataset someone else might have published.

On governance, I'd centralize row-level and object-level security once at the model level so every report built on top of it inherits the same rules automatically, rather than analysts reimplementing their own filters per report. Analysts connect live to this shared model (rather than copying data or recreating logic) to build their own visuals and layouts freely, which gives them the self-service speed leadership wants without giving them control over the underlying definitions. Critically, this isn't a one-time build: I'd establish a change-management process where the BI team owns and versions the model's measures, analysts request new measures be added centrally rather than inventing a 'shadow' version themselves, and I'd periodically audit the Service (via usage metrics, or simply searching for suspiciously named duplicate measures in personal workspaces) to catch drift early, backed by documentation - a data dictionary - and regular office hours so the certified model is easy to discover and use correctly instead of being bypassed out of convenience.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd frame this to leadership is that the fix for 'everyone building their own version of revenue' isn't tighter restrictions on self-service, it's giving people one well-built model so there's nothing left to reinvent. I'd build a single, centrally-owned semantic model with all the core measures already defined and named clearly, hide the raw columns nobody should be touching directly, and mark it Certified so it's obvious to every analyst which dataset is the real one to build from. RLS and object-level security get applied once, centrally, so every report built on top of it automatically inherits the same rules instead of each analyst reimplementing their own filters. Analysts then connect live to that model and build whatever reports and visuals they want - that's the self-service speed leadership is after - but they're not touching the underlying logic. The part I'd really push on is that this needs ongoing care, not a one-time build: the BI team owns and versions the measures, there's a documented way to request a new one instead of someone just inventing their own, and I'd periodically check the Service for duplicate 'Revenue' measures showing up in personal workspaces so drift gets caught early rather than discovered six months later in a leadership meeting.
commonMistakes: Exposing raw fact/dimension tables broadly and trusting analysts to compute consistent logic themselves
Not using certification/endorsement labels, leaving analysts unable to tell which dataset is authoritative
Applying RLS inconsistently per-report instead of once centrally in the shared model
Treating this as a one-time model build rather than an ongoing governance process with change management and drift monitoring
Not providing documentation or a data dictionary, leaving analysts to guess at measure definitions and reinvent them
keyPoints: Single certified, centrally-owned shared semantic model as the one source of truth
Hide raw columns, expose only curated, documented measures
Centralize RLS/OLS once at the model level
Endorsement (Certified/Promoted) for discoverability and trust
Ongoing governance: change management, drift monitoring, data dictionary, office hours

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a single governed shared model as the core design
Addresses hiding complexity and exposing curated measures
Addresses centralized RLS/security
Addresses certification/discoverability
Addresses ongoing governance process

questions.title: Defending a Type 2 Slowly Changing Dimension Against a 'Just Overwrite It' Proposal
questions.prompt: The business wants to analyze sales 'as it looked at the time' - attributing a historical sale to the customer's address at the time of purchase - but also wants an easy way to see all sales for a customer regardless of where they lived. A teammate proposes simply overwriting the CustomerAddress column whenever it changes, since it's simpler. Evaluate the proposal and recommend an approach.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd frame this as more than a 'simpler vs more complex' judgment call, because the overwrite approach (Type 1) doesn't just make the first requirement harder - it makes it impossible. If the address column is overwritten in place, every historical fact row's join to the Customer dimension reflects whatever the current address is at query time, regardless of when the sale actually happened; there is no way to recover 'what address was on file when this sale occurred' once the old value has been overwritten, because the history simply no longer exists anywhere in the model. That directly conflicts with the explicit requirement to analyze sales as they looked at the time, so this isn't really a tradeoff to debate - Type 1 fails a stated requirement outright.

I'd recommend a Type 2 design instead: each address change creates a new dimension row with its own surrogate key, an effective date, an expiry date (or null/high-date for the current row), and a current-flag, and each fact row at transaction time joins via the surrogate key representing whichever address was current then - that correctly supports the point-in-time analysis. For the second requirement, 'all sales regardless of address,' I'd make sure the dimension (and ideally the fact table too) also carries the durable, natural CustomerID alongside the surrogate key, so a query can group by that durable identifier across every historical version of the customer's record to get an address-agnostic view, while a query grouping by the surrogate key plus address gives the point-in-time view - both requirements are satisfied simultaneously by choosing which key to aggregate on. I'd be upfront that Type 2 isn't free: the ETL needs explicit change detection and row-expiry logic, the dimension table grows, and every downstream measure needs to be aware of which key it's joining on - but given that Type 1 can't meet the stated requirement at all, that complexity is a justified cost here, not a nice-to-have.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell my teammate directly that this isn't really a 'simpler is fine' situation, because overwriting the address doesn't just make history a little harder to get - it erases it completely. Once we overwrite CustomerAddress, every past sale's dimension join points at whatever address is current today, and there's no way to ask 'what address did this customer have when they bought this' anymore, which is literally the first thing the business asked for. So I'd push for a proper Type 2 design: new dimension row with its own surrogate key every time the address changes, effective and expiry dates, a current flag, and fact rows joining via the surrogate key that was current at transaction time - that gets us accurate point-in-time analysis. For the second ask, seeing all of a customer's sales regardless of address, I'd make sure we keep the durable CustomerID around too, so we can roll up by that across every version of the dimension row when someone wants the address-agnostic view. I wouldn't pretend this is free - it's real ETL work to detect changes and manage row expiry, and it's a bigger dimension table - but given that the overwrite approach can't deliver on one of the two things we were explicitly asked for, that cost isn't optional here.
commonMistakes: Choosing Type 1 for simplicity without recognizing it directly fails the 'as it looked at the time' requirement, not just making it less convenient
Implementing Type 2 but forgetting to retain a durable natural key, making the address-agnostic rollup requirement hard to satisfy
Not discussing the real ETL/complexity cost of Type 2 honestly
Confusing a Type 2 dimension with a separate audit/history log table that isn't actually joined to facts
Not considering that Type 2 is the correct answer here specifically because of the stated dual requirement, not as a default best practice
keyPoints: Type 1 overwrite cannot support point-in-time analysis at all - a hard requirement failure, not a tradeoff
Type 2 uses a surrogate key, effective/expiry dates, and a current flag to version history correctly
Retain the durable natural key for customer-level rollups regardless of address history
Both stated requirements are satisfied by choosing which key to aggregate on
Honestly acknowledge the real ETL/complexity cost of Type 2

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies Type 1 as failing the stated requirement outright, not just being less ideal
Recommends Type 2 with correct mechanics
Addresses retaining a durable key for cross-version rollup
Honestly discusses the complexity tradeoff
Clarity

questions.title: Deciding Where Transformation Logic Should Live: ETL vs ELT for a New Cloud Warehouse
questions.prompt: You're migrating a reporting workload off a legacy on-premises SQL Server that's used for both transactions and ad hoc reporting, causing contention, to a proper cloud warehouse. Decide between a traditional ETL approach (transforming before data lands) and an ELT approach (loading raw data first, transforming inside the warehouse with a tool like dbt), and justify your recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd separate two decisions that are getting conflated here. First, independent of ETL versus ELT, reporting simply has to stop hitting the production OLTP system directly - that system is built and tuned for high-concurrency small transactions, not large analytical scans, and the two workloads will keep conflicting on the same engine no matter which transformation philosophy we pick. Extracting to a dedicated analytical store is non-negotiable and happens either way.

On the actual ETL-versus-ELT question, I'd recommend ELT for a modern cloud warehouse. Cloud warehouses offer cheap, elastic compute specifically suited to running transformation inside the warehouse rather than in a separate, harder-to-scale ETL tool, and ELT means raw, untransformed data lands and persists in the warehouse as a landing/staging layer - which is genuinely valuable for auditability, for reprocessing when business logic changes later without re-extracting from a now-decoupled and possibly fragile source again, and for debugging, since you can always trace a transformed value back to its untouched raw form. A tool like dbt specifically adds version-controlled, tested, and documented transformation logic that runs in CI, which is much harder to replicate with logic buried inside an opaque ETL tool's mappings. The honest tradeoff is that ELT means potentially sensitive raw data lands in the warehouse before any cleansing or masking happens, so access control and row-level security need to be enforced at the transformed/mart layer (or even earlier, at the landing layer for highly sensitive fields) rather than assumed away; and the compute cost shifts from the ETL tool onto the warehouse's own consumption. I'd land on a layered ELT architecture - a raw/staging layer as extracted, then dbt-built intermediate and mart layers forming the actual star-schema facts and dimensions - with the OLTP system fully decoupled from any reporting traffic from day one.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I even get to ETL versus ELT, I'd point out that the contention problem is a separate issue that needs fixing regardless of which approach we pick - reporting has to stop hitting that OLTP system directly, period, because it's built for small fast transactions, not analytical scans, and that conflict doesn't go away just by choosing a transformation philosophy. Once that's settled, I'd lean ELT for the new cloud warehouse, mainly because cloud compute is cheap and elastic enough that transforming inside the warehouse with something like dbt just makes more sense than maintaining a separate transformation tool, and because keeping raw data around in a staging layer is genuinely useful - if business logic changes later, I can rebuild from raw without going back to a now-decoupled source system. dbt specifically gives us version control, tests, and documentation on the transformation logic that's much harder to get out of a traditional ETL tool's mappings. The honest tradeoff I'd flag is that raw, potentially sensitive data is now sitting in the warehouse before it's been cleaned up, so access control and masking need to happen at the mart layer or earlier - that's not optional just because we picked ELT. End state is a layered setup: raw staging, then dbt-built intermediate and mart layers forming the real star schema, with the old OLTP system completely out of the reporting path.
commonMistakes: Not addressing the OLTP contention problem as a separate, independent issue regardless of ETL/ELT choice
Treating ETL vs ELT as a stylistic coin-flip rather than connecting it to real cost and tooling realities
Not addressing security/access control implications of landing raw, unmasked data before transformation
Assuming ELT means skipping proper modeling, when a layered raw/staging/mart architecture is still required
Not mentioning testability, version control, or CI benefits of a dbt-driven ELT approach
keyPoints: Decoupling reporting from the OLTP system is a separate, non-negotiable fix regardless of ETL/ELT choice
ELT is favored for modern cloud warehouses due to elastic transform compute and tooling like dbt
A raw landing layer aids auditability and reprocessing when logic changes
A layered architecture (raw/staging -> intermediate -> mart) is still required under ELT
Security and access control must be addressed explicitly given raw data lands before cleansing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates the OLTP-decoupling issue from the ETL/ELT choice
Justifies ELT recommendation with concrete reasoning
Describes a proper layered architecture under ELT
Addresses security implications of raw data landing
Clarity

questions.title: Designing ALM for Power Automate Flows After an Untested Change Deleted Records
questions.prompt: Dozens of Power Automate flows were built directly in Production by business users, with no version control, no test environment, and a recent incident where an untested flow change deleted records it shouldn't have. Design an Application Lifecycle Management approach going forward.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start with actual environment separation - distinct Dev, Test, and Production Power Platform environments, not folders or naming conventions inside one shared environment - with flow development happening only in Dev going forward. The real ALM unit in the Power Platform is the Solution, so I'd package flows and their dependencies (connection references, and environment variables for things that differ per environment, like a SharePoint site URL or a SQL connection string) into solutions: unmanaged in Dev for active work, exported and imported as managed solutions into Test and then Production. This specifically prevents the kind of incident described, because a flow tested against Test's own data and connections is the exact same logical flow when it's promoted to Production - it isn't rebuilt by hand there, removing the main source of untested-in-production risk.

I'd automate the promotion itself using Power Platform Build Tools in Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions, exporting the solution from Dev and importing into Test then Production as a controlled pipeline with a required approval gate before the Production import, and I'd put the Dev solution's unpacked components under Git source control for history and rollback. On governance, I'd apply DLP policies and admin-center-level environment controls so business users can no longer build flows directly against Production connectors outside this pipeline, and specifically for the destructive-action risk that caused the actual incident, I'd require any flow performing deletes or other destructive changes to include an explicit approval step or more tightly scoped permissions, and mandate that any new logic touching production data be exercised against Test data first as a hard rule, not a suggestion.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd fix is that there's no real Dev/Test/Production separation here - that has to become actual separate Power Platform environments, not a convention. Then I'd get everything into Solutions, because that's genuinely how ALM works in this platform: environment variables and connection references inside the solution mean the same flow definition moves between environments without anyone manually rewiring connection strings each time, which directly closes the gap that let an untested change go straight into Production. I'd automate the actual promotion with Power Platform Build Tools in Azure DevOps, exporting from Dev and importing into Test then Prod with a required approval before that last step, and I'd keep the Dev solution's components in Git so we have real history. On the governance side, I'd lock down DLP and environment permissions so business users can't just build flows directly against Production connectors anymore. And specifically because the incident involved a destructive action, I'd put a hard rule in place that anything deleting or materially modifying records needs its own approval step and has to be proven against Test data first - that's non-negotiable given what already went wrong.
commonMistakes: Treating 'ALM' as just adding source control without adopting Solutions as the actual packaging/deployment unit
Not using environment variables/connection references, forcing manual reconfiguration (and risk) on every environment move
Not separating actual Dev/Test/Production environments, relying instead on folders or naming conventions
Not addressing governance/DLP to prevent the same ungoverned direct-to-Production editing from recurring
Not specifically addressing the destructive-action risk that caused the actual incident
keyPoints: Separate Dev/Test/Production Power Platform environments as the foundation
Solutions with environment variables and connection references as the ALM packaging unit
Automated solution deployment pipeline with a required approval gate before Production
Git source control for Dev solution components
Specific safeguards (approval, Test-data proof) for destructive actions given the actual incident

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes correct environment separation and Solutions-based ALM
Addresses environment variables/connection references specifically
Designs an automated deployment pipeline with approval gates
Addresses governance/DLP to prevent recurrence
Directly addresses the destructive-action incident

questions.title: Designing Secure Credential Management After a Data Factory Security Audit
questions.prompt: A security audit of your Data Factory environment found linked services with embedded SQL authentication connection strings, including a hardcoded password on one, and a service principal holding Owner on the entire subscription used for Blob Storage access. Design the correct credential and access architecture.
questions.modelAnswer:
For the hardcoded SQL password, the fix is to move it into Azure Key Vault and have the linked service reference it through Key Vault integration rather than storing it in plaintext in the pipeline definition or in any ARM template - that alone makes the credential centrally managed, rotatable, and no longer visible anywhere in source control or deployment artifacts. For the Blob Storage access using an Owner-scoped service principal, I'd go further than just better-hiding that credential: I'd replace it entirely with Data Factory's system-assigned (or user-assigned) managed identity, which removes the need to store or rotate a credential for that connection at all, since Azure handles the identity's authentication behind the scenes.

Whichever identity or service principal remains in use, I'd scope its RBAC role down to exactly what it needs at the narrowest resource boundary that works - Storage Blob Data Contributor on the specific storage account or container it actually touches, never Owner at the subscription level, which is wildly disproportionate to what a pipeline's data-movement activity actually requires. For SQL access specifically, I'd prefer Azure AD authentication via the managed identity where the target is Azure SQL, or if the source is on-premises SQL Server, I'd make sure the self-hosted integration runtime's own service account is tightly scoped and that whatever credential remains in Key Vault has a defined rotation and expiry policy rather than being set-and-forgotten. I'd close this out by removing the subscription-level Owner service principal entirely once the replacement access is validated, adding diagnostic logging and alerts on Key Vault access and linked-service changes to catch future drift, and scheduling a recurring (e.g., quarterly) access review so this becomes an ongoing control rather than a one-time cleanup following an audit finding.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the hardcoded password, that's the easy part to fix - move it into Key Vault and have the linked service pull it from there, so it's never sitting in plaintext in a pipeline definition or an ARM template again. The Owner-on-the-whole-subscription service principal is the part I'd actually spend more time on, because just hiding that credential better in Key Vault doesn't fix the underlying problem - the access itself is wildly overscoped. I'd replace it with Data Factory's managed identity wherever possible, so there's no stored credential at all for that connection, and then scope whatever RBAC role it actually needs down to the specific storage account, not the entire subscription. For SQL, I'd lean on Azure AD authentication through that same managed identity if it's Azure SQL, and if it's still on-prem, I'd make sure the self-hosted IR's service account and whatever's left in Key Vault has an actual rotation schedule instead of being set once and forgotten. And I wouldn't call this done after one cleanup pass - I'd want diagnostic alerts on Key Vault access and linked-service changes, plus a recurring access review, so this doesn't quietly drift back to where it started.
commonMistakes: Moving the password into Key Vault without also addressing the separately serious issue of subscription-level Owner scope
Not considering managed identity as a way to eliminate stored credentials entirely rather than just hiding them better
Granting a 'safer-sounding' but still overly broad role instead of the specific minimal RBAC role actually needed
Not planning credential rotation or an ongoing access review, treating this as a one-time cleanup
Not addressing authentication specifically for the on-premises SQL Server side
keyPoints: Key Vault-backed linked services eliminate plaintext/embedded credentials
Managed identity eliminates stored credentials for Blob Storage access entirely where supported
Scope RBAC to least privilege at the specific resource level, never subscription-level Owner
Prefer Azure AD authentication for SQL where possible
Establish ongoing credential rotation and periodic access review, not a one-time fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes Key Vault integration for remaining credentials
Proposes managed identity to eliminate stored credentials where possible
Correctly scopes RBAC to least privilege
Addresses ongoing rotation/review process
Clarity

questions.title: Designing a Permissions Model for 300 Tableau Workbooks Across 12 Departments
questions.prompt: A Tableau Server deployment has grown organically to 300+ workbooks across 12 departments, with permissions set ad hoc per-workbook by whoever published them. Some confidential HR dashboards ended up visible organization-wide, and some legitimate users can't find content they actually need. Design a governance and permissions model that fixes this at scale.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd move away from per-workbook permission decisions entirely and make the Project hierarchy the primary governance unit - nested Projects per department, with a further nested project for genuinely sensitive subsets like 'HR - Confidential' - and set permissions mainly at the project level using locked projects and permission templates, so content inherits consistent rules automatically instead of depending on whoever happened to publish it that day. I'd back that with Active Directory/SSO-backed group membership (department groups, plus a specific HR-Confidential security group) mapped to those project-level permission rules, so access changes become a group-membership change rather than someone manually clicking through 300 individual workbooks.

Sensitive projects get explicit default-deny treatment, with only the specific groups that need access granted View, while most departmental projects stay more broadly accessible within the organization for the sake of discoverability - which directly addresses the second half of the problem, that legitimate users can't find content they need. I'd pair that with a lightweight content-stewardship model: a small number of departmental stewards responsible for what gets published into shared, discoverable projects versus personal sandbox space, consistent naming/tagging conventions, and marking genuinely trusted workbooks as Certified so search surfaces the right content. Before rollout, I'd run a full audit of the existing 300 workbooks specifically to find and correct any ad hoc permissions that conflict with the new model - re-auditing the HR exposure incident and anything structurally similar first - and after rollout, I'd use Tableau Server's admin views for permission auditing and usage monitoring on an ongoing basis so this kind of drift gets caught early next time instead of becoming another incident.
questions.professionalAnswer: Trying to fix this workbook-by-workbook isn't going to hold up, so I'd restructure around Projects as the actual unit of governance - nested per department, with a locked-down nested project specifically for something like HR-Confidential - and set permissions mostly at that project level so new content just inherits the right rules instead of depending on whoever published it. I'd tie that to AD or SSO group membership rather than individual grants, so managing access becomes 'add this person to this group' instead of touching 300 separate workbooks. Sensitive projects get a hard default-deny with only the specific groups that need them let in, which directly fixes the HR exposure problem, and I'd keep most departmental projects more open so people can actually find what they need - which is the other half of the complaint here. I'd also put a little bit of process in place: departmental stewards who own what gets published broadly versus kept personal, consistent naming, and marking the genuinely trusted stuff as Certified so search works the way people expect. Before any of this goes live, I'd audit all 300 existing workbooks specifically looking for permissions that conflict with the new model, starting with anything that looks like the HR situation, and after that I'd keep using Tableau Server's admin views regularly so this doesn't quietly drift back to ad hoc again.
commonMistakes: Trying to fix this by auditing and correcting 300 individual workbooks' permissions one by one instead of restructuring around inherited project-level permissions
Not using AD/SSO group-based permission assignment, continuing to grant access to individual users ad hoc
Only addressing the security leak and ignoring that legitimate users can't find content they need
Not locking down sensitive projects with explicit default-deny
Treating this as a one-time cleanup rather than an ongoing governance process with stewardship and monitoring
keyPoints: Project-based permission hierarchy with locked projects as the sustainable governance unit
AD/SSO group-based permission assignment instead of ad hoc per-user or per-workbook grants
Explicit default-deny lockdown for sensitive content like HR
Content stewardship, naming conventions, and certification to fix discoverability
One-time audit of existing content plus ongoing drift monitoring

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a project-based permission hierarchy as the core fix
Proposes group-based access assignment
Directly addresses both the security leak and discoverability problems
Addresses audit and ongoing governance process

questions.title: Planning Power BI Workspace Structure and Licensing for 500 Report Consumers
questions.prompt: Your company is growing from 40 Power BI Pro users to a planned 500 report consumers across multiple departments, and leadership is asking whether to keep buying Pro licenses for everyone or move to a capacity-based model like Premium or Fabric. Walk through how you'd structure workspaces and make the licensing recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer:
On licensing, per-user Pro cost scales linearly with headcount, and at 500 consumers that gets expensive fast, especially since the vast majority of those 500 are likely pure viewers rather than content creators. Capacity-based licensing (Premium per-capacity, or a Fabric capacity SKU) decouples those two things: anyone can view content hosted in that capacity for free, and only the people actually authoring and publishing content need a Pro-equivalent license - so the real question is the ratio of creators to consumers, not the total headcount. If, say, 30-50 people actually build content and the rest are pure viewers, capacity-based licensing is very likely to win financially well before reaching 500 total users, and I'd actually run that crossover calculation with real numbers rather than relying on a rule of thumb. Capacity also unlocks capabilities Pro-only licensing simply doesn't offer at this scale regardless of cost - larger model sizes, far more frequent scheduled refresh, XMLA endpoint access, deployment pipelines, and paginated reports - all of which become relevant once the organization is operating at this size.

On workspace structure, I'd design a hierarchy aligned to department/function rather than one giant shared workspace, with each workspace having clearly designated owners and a governance point of contact, separate Dev/Test/Production workspaces per major solution feeding deployment pipelines, and a clear distinction between self-service sandbox workspaces (where broader edit access is fine) and curated/certified workspaces holding governed, widely-consumed content with tighter publish access and RLS/OLS applied. I'd plan capacity sizing and ongoing monitoring via the Fabric Capacity Metrics app to watch for throttling as 500 consumers' refreshes and interactive queries ramp up, with a scale-up/scale-down plan since capacity can be resized, and I'd recommend piloting the new SKU with a few departments first, measuring actual load, before rolling it out company-wide.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move would be to actually run the numbers rather than assume Pro licensing for 500 people is obviously too expensive or obviously fine - I'd figure out how many of those 500 are really content creators versus pure viewers, because capacity-based licensing lets viewers consume for free and only charges for the people actually building content. In most orgs that ratio is lopsided enough that capacity wins well before you hit 500 total users, and capacity also just unlocks things Pro can't give you at this scale - more frequent refresh, bigger models, the XMLA endpoint, deployment pipelines - so even setting cost aside, there's a real capability argument for moving at this size. On workspace structure, I wouldn't dump everything into one giant workspace - I'd build it out by department with clear owners, separate Dev/Test/Prod per major solution so we can use deployment pipelines properly, and a clear line between self-service sandbox spaces where people can experiment freely and the curated, governed workspaces that actually serve the business broadly. And before rolling a new capacity SKU out to everyone, I'd pilot it with a couple of departments first and watch the Fabric Capacity Metrics app to see real load before committing to a size for the whole company.
commonMistakes: Recommending continued per-user Pro licensing for all 500 without calculating the creator/consumer cost crossover
Not knowing capacity-based licensing allows free viewer access, treating 'more users' as only solvable by buying more Pro
Designing one flat workspace for the whole company rather than a department-aligned hierarchy with clear ownership
Not planning Dev/Test/Production separation at this scale
Not planning capacity monitoring/sizing, risking throttling once rolled out broadly
keyPoints: Capacity-based licensing separates creator cost from viewer cost, usually winning financially past a certain consumer count
Capacity unlocks features Pro-only licensing can't provide at scale (refresh frequency, XMLA, deployment pipelines, larger models)
Department-aligned workspace hierarchy with clear ownership and Dev/Test/Production separation
Distinguish self-service sandbox workspaces from curated/certified governed workspaces
Capacity monitoring via the Fabric Capacity Metrics app and a phased rollout

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons through Pro vs capacity licensing crossover
Identifies capacity-unlocked features relevant at this scale
Designs a sound workspace hierarchy with governance
Addresses capacity monitoring/phased rollout

questions.title: Department-Specific Data Marts or One Centralized Warehouse?
questions.prompt: Finance, Marketing, and Supply Chain each want their own fast, purpose-built reporting datasets, and each has proposed building and maintaining an independent data mart with its own ETL rather than working off a shared central warehouse, arguing it's faster for their team to control end-to-end. As the senior analytics engineer, how do you respond, and what architecture do you recommend?
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start by validating the real concern driving this proposal rather than dismissing it outright: departments want speed and control, and a fully centralized model where one team is the bottleneck for every single change request is a genuine, common failure mode that pushes people toward exactly this kind of workaround - if I just overrule them, I should expect shadow-IT marts to spring up anyway. That said, I'd push back on fully independent, siloed marts with separate ETL per department, because it recreates the problems a shared source of truth exists to prevent: three different definitions of 'Customer' or 'Revenue' that quietly drift apart across Finance's, Marketing's, and Supply Chain's separate pipelines, duplicated extraction load hitting the same source systems three times, and three times the engineering effort maintaining parallel ETL that's mostly doing the same underlying work.

My recommendation is the standard hub-and-spoke compromise: a centrally-owned, conformed layer where shared dimensions - Customer, Product, Date/Calendar - are built once and reused everywhere, feeding department-specific marts (physical tables or virtual views/semantic models) that layer each department's own business logic on top, owned and iterated on by each department's own analysts. This gives departments the speed and autonomy they're actually asking for at the mart layer, while guaranteeing the core shared entities and metrics stay consistent across the organization at the conformed layer underneath. Practically, I'd propose the central team own extraction and the conformed dimension/fact layer with clear SLAs for adding new source data, departments own and can rapidly iterate on their own mart-layer models without waiting on the central team for every change, and a lightweight governance forum where any new shared definition gets vetted into the conformed layer instead of being reinvented three separate times.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just tell them no, because the frustration behind this proposal is legitimate - nobody wants to wait on a central team for every small change, and if I just mandate one fully centralized warehouse with my team as the gatekeeper for everything, I'd expect shadow marts to show up anyway, just without my visibility into them. But I also wouldn't agree to three fully independent marts with their own ETL, because that's exactly how you end up with three different definitions of Revenue quietly drifting apart, plus three pipelines hitting the same source systems and tripling the engineering effort for work that's mostly identical. What I'd actually propose is a hub-and-spoke setup - a centrally-owned conformed layer with shared dimensions like Customer, Product, and Date built once, feeding department-owned marts on top where Finance, Marketing, and Supply Chain can move fast and control their own business logic without needing my team in the loop for every change. They get the speed and autonomy they're asking for at their layer, and we guarantee consistency underneath at the conformed layer. I'd also set up a lightweight process so when someone needs a new shared definition, it gets added to the conformed layer once instead of getting reinvented three separate times.
commonMistakes: Overruling the departments and mandating one fully centralized warehouse with the central team as gatekeeper for every change, ignoring the legitimate autonomy/speed concern
Agreeing to fully independent per-department marts without addressing definitional drift and duplicated engineering effort
Not knowing the conformed-dimension, hub-and-spoke pattern as the standard resolution to this exact conflict
Not proposing a concrete governance process for how new shared definitions get added to the central layer
Treating this as a purely technical question rather than also an organizational/process design question
keyPoints: Validate the legitimate autonomy/speed concern rather than dismissing it outright
Fully independent marts risk definitional drift and duplicated ETL/extraction load
Hub-and-spoke architecture with a centrally-owned conformed dimension/fact layer feeding department-owned marts
Departments get speed and autonomy at the mart layer, consistency is guaranteed at the conformed layer
A lightweight governance process is needed for adding new shared definitions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Acknowledges the legitimate departmental concern rather than dismissing it
Correctly identifies the risks of fully independent marts
Proposes a conformed-dimension hub-and-spoke architecture
Proposes a concrete governance/ownership split
Clarity
